fencing.intro: Fencing: boundary, security and garden fencing chosen from a measured site survey. iComply works for homeowners, landlords, managing agents and businesses from its Stockport workshop, measures before it specifies, and quotes every job price on application. It sets out the options, the specification choices and the questions worth asking before you commit to fencing.
fencing.body:
This page is the starting point for fencing with iComply. It compares the main families of fence, explains how a site survey turns a rough idea into a written specification, and links to the detailed guides for palisade, mesh, closeboard, railings, temporary fencing and gates so you can go deeper on the option that fits your boundary.

Fencing covers a wide range of products, from a featheredge garden boundary to a 3 m steel palisade line around a depot. The right choice starts with what the fence has to do: mark a boundary, keep people or animals in, keep intruders out, screen a view, reduce noise or protect children. Once the job is clear, the height, material, post system and gate positions follow from the ground and the length measured on site.

Boundary lines are confirmed by the owner before a post goes in. Where a fence replaces an older one, the new line normally follows the old post positions unless the owner says otherwise. Where neighbours share a boundary, the owner is encouraged to agree the line and the finished face first. iComply fences the line it is shown and does not decide a legal boundary.

Most fencing enquiries fall into three families. Timber fencing such as closeboard, panel and post-and-rail suits gardens, communal areas and screening. Steel mesh and palisade suit commercial and industrial boundaries where strength and visibility matter. Railings suit frontages, schools and public spaces where a fence must look tidy for decades. Mixed sites often use more than one family, and the scope says where each run starts and stops.

Ground conditions drive more of the cost and the lifespan than most people expect. Clay, made ground, tree roots, buried services, slopes and hard surfaces all change how posts are set. Posts are concreted, driven or base-plated to suit what is found when the line is walked, and a trial hole is dug where the ground is unknown rather than guessing a foundation depth.

Planning rules, boundary agreements and lease terms can all affect fencing. Height near a highway, conservation areas, listed buildings, planning conditions on newer estates and covenants on some properties are worth checking early. iComply flags the points it sees; the owner makes the checks and decisions.

Most buyers underestimate how much the ground affects the job. A level lawn, a sloping bank, a tarmac car park and a strip of made ground beside a building all need different post and foundation methods. Asking how the posts will be set, and what happens if buried services or old concrete are found, avoids surprises.

Lifespan depends on the material and the care it gets. Timber needs treatment and will eventually need parts replaced. Galvanised and powder-coated steel lasts much longer with little maintenance. Asking what maintenance the chosen option needs, and how often, is part of choosing well.

Before choosing fencing, it helps to write down what the boundary must achieve. Privacy, security, keeping children or animals in, marking a line, screening bins or plant, and meeting a landlord's or insurer's requirement all point to different products. A short list of priorities makes the survey quicker and the recommendation clearer.

The specification for fencing is usually described in a handful of terms: height, material, profile or panel type, post type and foundation, finish and colour, and gate details. When comparing quotes, checking each of those terms side by side shows whether two prices are for the same thing.

Installation of fencing starts with setting out. The line is marked with pegs and a string line from the confirmed boundary points, corners and gate positions. Panel or bay widths are worked out from the ends so cut sections fall where they are least visible, and the post positions are marked before any digging starts.

Installation time depends on the length, the ground, access and the weather. The plan agreed in the scope sets out the sequence and any phasing, and the client is kept informed if conditions on the day change the plan.

Before digging, the line is checked for buried services using utility drawings where available and a cable avoidance tool. Where services are suspected, holes are dug by hand. Old foundations, roots and rubble found in the ground are dealt with as they are found, and any change to the plan is agreed.

Typical palisade heights are 1.8 m, 2.1 m, 2.4 m and 3.0 m, with lower and taller options in some ranges. The height affects the number of rails, the post size and the foundation. A 3.0 m run carries noticeably more load from its own weight and from people leaning or climbing than a 1.8 m run, so the posts and concrete are sized accordingly.

A capping rail and counter batten along the top throw rainwater off the end grain of the boards and add a finished look. Both are optional but are worth including on a fence that is meant to last. Post caps do the same job for timber posts.

Landlords and agents often need fencing work coordinated with tenants. Access dates, keys, pets and parking are agreed in advance, and photos of the finished work can be supplied for the property file.

Homeowners usually want a fence that looks good, gives privacy and lasts. Landlords and managing agents want something durable and easy to maintain across several properties. Businesses want security and a tidy frontage. The same survey approach works for all of them, with the specification adjusted to suit.

Mixed-use sites, such as flats above shops or yards behind offices, often need more than one fence type: a secure service yard, a tidy frontage and a private garden area. The scope sets out each run separately.

Shared boundaries are common in terraced and semi-detached housing. Agreeing the line, the height and the finished face with the neighbour before work starts avoids disputes later. The owner makes that agreement; iComply fences to the line it is given.

iComply does not promise attendance or completion times in advance. Visits and installation dates are agreed directly with you, and you are kept informed if weather or ground conditions change the plan on the day.

iComply Property Services works from a workshop at 17 Woodlands Park Road, Offerton, Stockport, Cheshire SK2 5DE. Fencing enquiries can be sent by phone or WhatsApp on 07517 806082, or by email to info@icomplypropertyservices.co.uk, with the site address, a few photos and a rough idea of the length and height.

Where a specification, insurer or landlord sets requirements for a fence, the scope refers to them and the products are chosen to meet them. Certification of a product belongs to its manufacturer; iComply supplies and installs to the maker's instructions.

Every fencing job is quoted price on application. The quote follows a survey or a review of clear photos and measurements and is based on a written scope, so you can see exactly what is included before agreeing to anything.

faq: Do I need planning permission for a new fence?

Many fences do not, but height limits apply in some positions, such as next to a highway, and listed buildings, conservation areas or planning conditions can change things. We flag where a check with the local planning authority is sensible; the owner makes that check.
How long does fencing last?

It depends on the material, the finish, the ground and the exposure. Treated timber lasts longer with regular preservative, and galvanised or powder-coated steel lasts far longer than bare steel. The scope states the finish so expectations are clear.
What should I decide before getting a quote?
Write down what the fence must achieve, the rough length and height you have in mind, and any gates. The survey then confirms the details and the right specification.
Why is there no price list?
Cost depends on length, height, ground, access and specification. Every job is quoted price on application from a written scope.
Do you work for landlords and managing agents?
Yes. We coordinate access with tenants and can supply photos of completed work for your records.

Security fencing is any fence chosen mainly to delay or deter intrusion rather than simply mark a boundary. Ground clearance is a common weak point. A gap under a fence on uneven ground lets people crawl under and lets animals in. Panels are set close to the ground, and where levels change, the base is filled or the fence is stepped carefully so no large gap is left at the bottom.

Delay is the honest way to think about a security fence. No fence stops a determined intruder with tools indefinitely; a good fence makes climbing and cutting slower, noisier and more visible, which gives cameras, alarms and people time to act. Posts are the most common repair. Rotten timber posts are replaced or supported with concrete repair spurs, and leaning steel or concrete posts are reset in new foundations. Where many posts along a run have failed, replacing the run is usually better value than repairing post by post.

Storm damage often affects several bays at once. Panels blown out, posts snapped at ground level and gates wrenched off their hinges are common after high winds. Making the boundary safe comes first, followed by a permanent repair once materials are available.

Many repairs are local. Single panels, boards, pales, mesh panels, rails and fixings can usually be replaced without disturbing the rest of the line, provided matching parts are available. The repair is matched to the existing material, height and finish as closely as possible.

Repairs involving steel include treating any cut, drilled or welded areas with a zinc-rich primer or cold galvanising before any topcoat. Leaving bare steel exposed causes rust to spread under the remaining coating.

There are two main pale profiles. D-section pales are a curved, D-shaped section suited to lower-risk boundaries and general demarcation. mesh-fencing.body:

Visibility is one of the main reasons to choose mesh over palisade. A mesh fence lets people, cameras and patrols see through the boundary, which suits car parks, schools, play areas and sites with CCTV. The trade-off is that the mesh aperture and wire thickness decide how easy it is to climb or cut, so the panel is chosen for the risk.

Mesh panel systems usually have three parts: the panel, the post and the clamp or fixing that joins them. Posts may be rectangular hollow section or proprietary profiles with clamp bars that hold the panel edges. The system is installed as a matched set from one manufacturer so the clamps, posts and panels fit together as designed.

Mesh fencing is a broad term for fences made of steel wire mesh, either welded into rigid panels or woven into rolls. Rigid welded mesh panel systems are the modern standard for commercial boundaries, schools and sports areas, while woven chain link still suits some low-cost and temporary needs. The panel type, wire gauge, aperture and height are what define a mesh fence.

Common panel types include 358 mesh for high security, 868 twin-wire for strong general-purpose boundaries, 656 twin-wire for lighter duties, and V-mesh or rigid single-wire panels with pressed folds for everyday commercial use. Each has a different aperture and wire specification, which the scope names rather than using a generic description.

Mesh panels are set with a small, even gap above the ground. On slopes, rigid panels are usually stepped, so the posts are set at different heights and each panel stays level; the triangular gaps below are filled or closed with a kicker board where needed so the fence does not leave a crawl space.

A written scope protects both sides. It lists what is included, what is excluded, how waste is removed, how the site is left and what happens if something unexpected is found. With mesh fencing, as with most building work, the clearer the scope, the fewer disagreements at the end.

iComply quotes mesh fencing price on application after a survey or after reviewing clear photos and measurements. There are no headline prices, because the cost depends on length, height, ground, access and specification, all of which differ from site to site.

Lifespan depends on the material and the care it gets. Timber needs treatment and will eventually need parts replaced. Galvanised and powder-coated steel lasts much longer with little maintenance. Asking what maintenance the chosen option needs, and how often, is part of choosing well.

Before choosing mesh fencing, it helps to write down what the boundary must achieve. Privacy, security, keeping children or animals in, marking a line, screening bins or plant, and meeting a landlord's or insurer's requirement all point to different products. A short list of priorities makes the survey quicker and the recommendation clearer.

Facilities managers need fencing work that fits around the business. Out-of-hours working, phased installation, clear method statements and a tidy site at the end of each day are normal requirements and are agreed before work starts.

Insurers sometimes ask for specific security measures as a condition of cover. Where an insurer or security consultant has set a requirement, the fence is specified to meet it, and the scope refers to the requirement.

Commercial customers often need documents for their own records: insurance details, risk assessments, method statements and product information. Those are provided as part of the job.

Many commercial premises are leased. Tenants should check lease terms and landlord consent before changing a boundary, and managing agents often want a written specification for approval. The scope is written to support that process.

Weldmesh fencing uses panels of steel wire welded at every intersection to form a rigid grid. The panels are fixed to posts with clamp bars or brackets.

Weldmesh fencing is installed with posts set in concrete at the panel spacing, panels lifted into place and clamped, and posts plumbed as the run progresses. Clamp-bar posts hold the panel edges between the post and a continuous flat bar, fixed with security bolts. This spreads the load along the panel edge and makes the panels harder to remove from outside. Where security matters, the bolts are a tamper-resistant type and face into the site.

Weldmesh panels are specified by wire diameter, aperture size and panel height. Posts are the most common repair. Rotten timber posts are replaced or supported with concrete repair spurs, and leaning steel or concrete posts are reset in new foundations. Where many posts along a run have failed, replacing the run is usually better value than repairing post by post.

Heights for 358 systems commonly run from about 2.0 m to 3.0 m and above, depending on the manufacturer's range. 358 panels are heavy and rigid, so they are fixed to strong posts with continuous clamp bars and security bolts. On higher-risk sites, a double-skin arrangement or a second layer at the bottom of the fence is sometimes specified to add delay. Toppings such as razor wire or rotating spikes can be added where they are justified and signed.

358 mesh fencing takes its name from its aperture in imperial measurements: roughly 3 inches by 0.5 inch, which works out at about 76.2 mm by 12.7 mm, using 8-gauge wire of about 4 mm. The very small horizontal gap means fingers and boot toes cannot get a grip, and standard hand tools struggle to get a purchase on the wire.

Because of that small aperture, 358 mesh is often called prison mesh or anti-climb mesh. It is widely used on high-security boundaries such as utility sites, data and telecoms compounds, transport depots, schools with specific security needs and commercial premises where intrusion is a known risk.

From a distance, 358 mesh looks almost solid, but up close it stays see-through, which keeps sightlines for CCTV and patrols. This is one of its advantages over palisade where camera coverage across the boundary matters.

A repair quote sets out what has failed, why, what is being replaced and what is being left. Where the remaining parts are near the end of their life, the quote says so honestly, so the decision between repair and replacement is an informed one.

Vehicle damage on commercial and industrial sites tends to bend posts, rails and pales. Bent steel is replaced rather than straightened where its strength or finish has been compromised, and protection such as bollards or barriers is suggested where impacts keep happening.

Repairs involving steel include treating any cut, drilled or welded areas with a zinc-rich primer or cold galvanising before any topcoat. Leaving bare steel exposed causes rust to spread under the remaining coating.

Repairs to 358 mesh fencing start with finding the cause. A leaning section, a broken panel or a sagging gate may come from a failed post, a loose fixing, wind damage, vehicle impact, tree roots or simple age. Fixing the cause matters, otherwise the same failure returns.

Posts are the most common repair. Rotten timber posts are replaced or supported with concrete repair spurs, and leaning steel or concrete posts are reset in new foundations. Where many posts along a run have failed, replacing the run is usually better value than repairing post by post.

868-twin-wire-mesh-fencing-repair.intro: This guide to 868 Twin-Wire Mesh Fencing Repair explains twin horizontal wires either side of each vertical for a stiff, flat, durable panel, what decides the right approach for school business managers, academy trusts, nurseries and estates teams, and how iComply scopes the work before anything is ordered. It covers how damage is assessed, when a repair is sensible and when replacement is the better value.
868-twin-wire-mesh-fencing-repair.body:
Twin-wire panels are tough, but ball strikes, vehicle impacts and vandalism can still bend them. This page explains how 868 panels are replaced with matching panels from the same range and how posts and fixings are restored.

868 twin-wire mesh fencing uses pairs of 8 mm horizontal wires either side of 6 mm vertical wires, which is where the name comes from. The double horizontal wires make a flat panel that is very stiff without needing folds, and the aperture is typically about 200 mm by 50 mm. It is a popular choice for schools, sports facilities, business parks and public spaces.

Twin-wire fences need little maintenance. Checks cover fixings, post plumb, coating damage, vegetation growing through and any gap opening under the panels. Damaged panels are replaced with a matching panel from the same range.

868 panels are fixed to posts with clamp bars or brackets, usually galvanised and powder coated to match the mesh. Posts are set in concrete at the panel width. Gates in matching twin-wire infill are available for pedestrian and vehicle openings, with manual hinges and locks.

The aperture of 868 mesh is larger than 358, so it is easier to climb. On higher-risk boundaries, 868 is combined with toppings or a taller fence, or 358 is specified instead. The survey and scope make that choice explicit.

Twin-wire panels are strong enough to resist ball strikes and leaning crowds, which is why they are used for ball-stop fencing around pitches and MUGAs at taller heights. The panel can be supplied with the vertical wires projecting at the top, or flush, which affects both the look and the comfort of anyone touching the top of the fence.

656 twin-wire uses the same layout with lighter wires, 6 mm horizontal pairs and 5 mm verticals, for boundaries where 868 strength is not needed. Both are installed the same way, but they are not interchangeable in a specification, so the scope names which one is being supplied.

Repairs to 868 twin-wire mesh fencing start with finding the cause. A leaning section, a broken panel or a sagging gate may come from a failed post, a loose fixing, wind damage, vehicle impact, tree roots or simple age. Fixing the cause matters, otherwise the same failure returns.

Posts are the most common repair. Rotten timber posts are replaced or supported with concrete repair spurs, and leaning steel or concrete posts are reset in new foundations. Where many posts along a run have failed, replacing the run is usually better value than repairing post by post.

Many repairs are local. Single panels, boards, pales, mesh panels, rails and fixings can usually be replaced without disturbing the rest of the line, provided matching parts are available. The repair is matched to the existing material, height and finish as closely as possible.

Insurance claims for fence damage often need photos and a written description. iComply can provide photos of the damage and a written scope and quote to support a claim; the claim itself is between the owner and the insurer.

Storm damage often affects several bays at once. Panels blown out, posts snapped at ground level and gates wrenched off their hinges are common after high winds. Making the boundary safe comes first, followed by a permanent repair once materials are available.

On sites where the boundary cannot be left open, replacement is phased so only a short section is down at any time, or temporary fencing is used until the new line is complete.

Replacing 868 twin-wire mesh fencing usually follows the old line unless the owner confirms a change. Where the old fence was on a shared boundary, the owner is encouraged to agree the replacement with the neighbour first, including the height and which way the finished face points.

Replacement means taking down an existing fence and putting a new one up along the agreed line. It is the right choice when the posts have failed along much of the run, when the material has reached the end of its life, or when the owner wants a different type of fence.

Mesh panels are set with a small, even gap above the ground. On slopes, rigid panels are usually stepped, so the posts are set at different heights and each panel stays level; the triangular gaps below are filled or closed with a kicker board where needed so the fence does not leave a crawl space.

Weldmesh fencing is installed with posts set in concrete at the panel spacing, panels lifted into place and clamped, and posts plumbed as the run progresses. Panel widths are fixed, so the run is set out from the ends and corners first, with a cut panel where the length requires one, treated where it is cut.

Work at schools is planned around term dates, the school run and safeguarding procedures. Holiday and out-of-hours working is common, and operatives follow sign-in and site rules.

Academy trusts and local authorities often need detailed written quotes and specifications for funding and procurement. The scope is written to support those processes.

Durability and low maintenance matter for school budgets. Galvanised and powder-coated mesh and railings last many years with little upkeep, which is why they are the usual choice for school boundaries.

Schools and nurseries need fencing that supports safeguarding: a continuous secure line, controlled entrances, no gaps and no climbing aids. The layout is agreed with the school's leadership and estates team.

Work is carried out with risk assessments appropriate to the job, care around buried services and protection for lawns, paving and planting next to the line. Operatives follow site rules and inductions on commercial, school and industrial premises.

Every fencing job is quoted price on application. The quote follows a survey or a review of clear photos and measurements and is based on a written scope, so you can see exactly what is included before agreeing to anything.

closeboard-fencing.body:
Closeboard fencing is built board by board on site, which gives it strength and lets it follow the ground. This page explains featheredge boards, arris and cant rails, timber and concrete posts, gravel boards and the capping details that help a closeboard fence last.

Posts for closeboard are usually treated timber or slotted concrete. Timber posts are commonly 100 mm square for standard heights, and concrete posts with mortices take arris rails and last longer at ground level. A gravel board at the base, in timber or concrete, keeps the featheredge boards off the soil so they do not wick up moisture and rot.

A capping rail and counter batten along the top throw rainwater off the end grain of the boards and add a finished look. Both are optional but are worth including on a fence that is meant to last. Post caps do the same job for timber posts.

Closeboard fencing, sometimes called featheredge fencing, is built on site rather than delivered as ready-made panels. Posts are set in the ground, two or three horizontal rails are fixed between them, and vertical featheredge boards are nailed to the rails so each board overlaps the next. The result is a solid, strong screen that copes with wind better than most panels.

Because it is built board by board, closeboard follows the ground. On a slope the rails can be raked so the top of the fence runs parallel to the ground, with no stepped gaps underneath. Run lengths do not have to match a panel width, which helps on awkward boundaries, corners and short returns.

Treated timber still needs looking after. Pressure-treated boards weather to silver-grey unless they are stained. A preservative or stain every few years extends the life of the fence, and keeping soil and planting off the boards helps more than most treatments.

Before choosing closeboard fencing, it helps to write down what the boundary must achieve. Privacy, security, keeping children or animals in, marking a line, screening bins or plant, and meeting a landlord's or insurer's requirement all point to different products. A short list of priorities makes the survey quicker and the recommendation clearer.

Most buyers underestimate how much the ground affects the job. A level lawn, a sloping bank, a tarmac car park and a strip of made ground beside a building all need different post and foundation methods. Asking how the posts will be set, and what happens if buried services or old concrete are found, avoids surprises.

A written scope protects both sides. It lists what is included, what is excluded, how waste is removed, how the site is left and what happens if something unexpected is found. With closeboard fencing, as with most building work, the clearer the scope, the fewer disagreements at the end.

The specification for closeboard fencing is usually described in a handful of terms: height, material, profile or panel type, post type and foundation, finish and colour, and gate details. When comparing quotes, checking each of those terms side by side shows whether two prices are for the same thing.

Height near a highway, conservation areas, listed buildings, planning conditions on newer estates and covenants on some properties are worth checking early. iComply flags the points it sees; the owner makes the checks and decisions.

Repairs involving steel include treating any cut, drilled or welded areas with a zinc-rich primer or cold galvanising before any topcoat. Leaving bare steel exposed causes rust to spread under the remaining coating.

Looking at the posts first tells you whether the job is a repair, a part replacement or a new line, and that decision is written down before anything is ordered.

Wind is the main enemy of panel fences. A solid panel acts like a sail, and lightweight lap panels can blow out on exposed boundaries. Posts are set to the depth and foundation the system and the ground require. They are set plumb in both directions and in line, and braced while concrete cures. Getting the posts right is most of the job, because everything else hangs from them.

Installation of closeboard fencing starts with setting out. The line is marked with pegs and a string line from the confirmed boundary points, corners and gate positions. Panel or bay widths are worked out from the ends so cut sections fall where they are least visible, and the post positions are marked before any digging starts.

Installation time depends on the length, the ground, access and the weather. The plan agreed in the scope sets out the sequence and any phasing, and the client is kept informed if conditions on the day change the plan.

Gates are hung once their posts have set firm. Hinges, latches, stops and drop bolts are fitted, and the gate is adjusted so it swings freely and closes properly. A gate that is hung on posts before the concrete has cured will often drop later.

To get an accurate quote quickly, send the address, the approximate length and height, photos of the boundary and any gates, and a note of what you want the fence to achieve. A written scope and quote follow, listing what is included.

closeboard-fencing-repair.intro: Closeboard Fencing Repair from iComply Property Services covers overlapping featheredge boards on arris or cant rails, built in place along the line. This guide is written for homeowners, landlords and residents' management companies and starts from a site survey and a written scope, not a catalogue price. It covers how damage is assessed, when a repair is sensible and when replacement is the better value.
closeboard-fencing-repair.body:
Closeboard fencing can often be repaired rather than replaced. This page explains how broken arris rails, split boards, rotten gravel boards and failed posts are dealt with, and when the fence as a whole has reached the end of its life.

Because it is built board by board, closeboard follows the ground. On a slope the rails can be raked so the top of the fence runs parallel to the ground, with no stepped gaps underneath. Run lengths do not have to match a panel width, which helps on awkward boundaries, corners and short returns.

Closeboard repairs are often possible without taking the fence down. Broken arris rails can be strengthened with galvanised repair brackets or replaced, split boards can be swapped one at a time, and rotten gravel boards replaced. Where the posts themselves have rotted, setting new posts or concrete spurs is usually the lasting answer.

A capping rail and counter batten along the top throw rainwater off the end grain of the boards and add a finished look. Both are optional but are worth including on a fence that is meant to last. Post caps do the same job for timber posts.

Rails are either arris rails, which are triangular in section, or cant rails, which are a sloping rectangular section. Three rails are normal for fences around 1.8 m high. Boards are typically featheredge of about 100 mm to 125 mm wide, overlapped by around 25 mm, and fixed with galvanised or stainless nails so they do not streak or rust.

Treated timber still needs looking after. Pressure-treated boards weather to silver-grey unless they are stained. A preservative or stain every few years extends the life of the fence, and keeping soil and planting off the boards helps more than most treatments.

Posts for closeboard are usually treated timber or slotted concrete. Timber posts are commonly 100 mm square for standard heights, and concrete posts with mortices take arris rails and last longer at ground level. A gravel board at the base, in timber or concrete, keeps the featheredge boards off the soil so they do not wick up moisture and rot.

Many repairs are local. Single panels, boards, pales, mesh panels, rails and fixings can usually be replaced without disturbing the rest of the line, provided matching parts are available. The repair is matched to the existing material, height and finish as closely as possible.

Insurance claims for fence damage often need photos and a written description. iComply can provide photos of the damage and a written scope and quote to support a claim; the claim itself is between the owner and the insurer.

A repair quote sets out what has failed, why, what is being replaced and what is being left. Where the remaining parts are near the end of their life, the quote says so honestly, so the decision between repair and replacement is an informed one.

Vehicle damage on commercial and industrial sites tends to bend posts, rails and pales. Bent steel is replaced rather than straightened where its strength or finish has been compromised, and protection such as bollards or barriers is suggested where impacts keep happening.

Repairs to closeboard fencing start with finding the cause. A leaning section, a broken panel or a sagging gate may come from a failed post, a loose fixing, wind damage, vehicle impact, tree roots or simple age. Fixing the cause matters, otherwise the same failure returns.

Most buyers underestimate how much the ground affects the job. A level lawn, a sloping bank, a tarmac car park and a strip of made ground beside a building all need different post and foundation methods. Asking how the posts will be set, and what happens if buried services or old concrete are found, avoids surprises.

Before choosing closeboard fencing, it helps to write down what the boundary must achieve. Privacy, security, keeping children or animals in, marking a line, screening bins or plant, and meeting a landlord's or insurer's requirement all point to different products. A short list of priorities makes the survey quicker and the recommendation clearer.

Good access makes installation simpler. Clear routes for materials, somewhere to unload, room to work on both sides of the line and a plan for any planting or structures near the boundary all help. The survey notes access so the plan is realistic.

Panels are fixed either to timber posts with brackets or screws, or slotted into the grooves of concrete posts. Concrete slotted posts with concrete gravel boards are the most durable option at ground level, because nothing timber touches the soil, and panels can be lifted out and replaced without disturbing the posts.

Steel posts for mesh and palisade systems follow the manufacturer's size, spacing and foundation guidance. Base-plated posts are bolted to existing concrete or slabs where digging is not possible, using fixings chosen for the base, and are only used where the base can take the load.

Residential access is often tight. Materials may need carrying through a side passage or even through the house, and gardens need protecting during the work. Access is noted at the survey so the plan is realistic.

Residents' management companies and landlords often look after shared boundaries on estates and blocks. Consistency of style across the estate, tenant access and budgets for planned work are part of the conversation.

For homes, a fence is part of the garden as much as the boundary. Height, style, colour and how it suits planting and paving matter as much as strength. A survey covers the look you want as well as the practical needs.

Pets and children affect the specification. Gaps under fences, gates that do not close properly and climbable rails are the usual concerns, and the scope addresses them directly.

Neighbours share most residential boundaries. Talking to the neighbour before work starts, agreeing the line and height, and deciding which way the finished face points all help the job go smoothly.

Work is carried out with risk assessments appropriate to the job, care around buried services and protection for lawns, paving and planting next to the line. Operatives follow site rules and inductions on commercial, school and industrial premises.

faq: Do I need my neighbour's permission?
For a fence on your own land, usually not, but agreeing the line and finished face with your neighbour avoids disputes. Shared boundaries need agreement.
Is closeboard stronger than fence panels?
Generally, yes. Closeboard is built in place on rails fixed to posts, so it resists wind and impact better than most lightweight panels.
Can closeboard follow a slope?
Yes. The rails can be raked to follow the ground, so the fence runs smoothly down a slope without stepped gaps.
Do I need gravel boards?
They are strongly recommended. A gravel board keeps the featheredge boards off the soil, which slows rot and makes the base easier to replace later.
Is it worth repairing or should I replace?

If most of the posts and panels are sound, repair is usually sensible. If many posts have failed or the materials are near the end of their life, replacement is often better value. The quote explains which.

Panel fence repairs are usually about replacing blown or rotten panels, swapping split timber posts for concrete, or setting a leaning post upright. Where only one or two panels have failed, matching the style and colour of the remaining fence is part of the job.

Panel quality varies widely. Thicker boards, heavier frames and pressure treatment rather than dip treatment make a real difference to lifespan. The scope names the panel style and treatment so the quote can be compared fairly.

Panel fencing uses ready-made timber panels, usually 1.83 m wide, fixed between posts. It is quick to install and familiar in gardens and communal areas. Common panel styles include lap or waney-edge panels, closeboard-style panels, tongue-and-groove, slatted contemporary panels and decorative trellis tops.

Panels are fixed either to timber posts with brackets or screws, or slotted into the grooves of concrete posts. Concrete slotted posts with concrete gravel boards are the most durable option at ground level, because nothing timber touches the soil, and panels can be lifted out and replaced without disturbing the posts.

Panel fences on slopes are stepped, with each panel level and the posts set at different heights. The triangular gaps below are filled with gravel boards cut to suit. That stepped look suits some gardens and not others, and the alternative of a raked closeboard fence is mentioned where it fits better.

Wind is the main enemy of panel fences. A solid panel acts like a sail, and lightweight lap panels can blow out on exposed boundaries. On windy sites, heavier closeboard-style panels, slatted panels that let some air through, or a closeboard fence built in place are better choices. The survey notes exposure before a panel is chosen.

Panel fencing repairs usually involve blown-out panels, rotten timber posts or leaning concrete posts. This page explains how each is put right, how new panels are matched and when converting to concrete posts makes sense.

Panels are fixed either to timber posts with brackets or screws, or slotted into the grooves of concrete posts. Concrete slotted posts with concrete gravel boards are the most durable option at ground level, because nothing timber touches the soil, and panels can be lifted out and replaced without disturbing the posts.

Panel fences on slopes are stepped, with each panel level and the posts set at different heights. The triangular gaps below are filled with gravel boards cut to suit. That stepped look suits some gardens and not others, and the alternative of a raked closeboard fence is mentioned where it fits better.

Wind is the main enemy of panel fences. A solid panel acts like a sail, and lightweight lap panels can blow out on exposed boundaries. On windy sites, heavier closeboard-style panels, slatted panels that let some air through, or a closeboard fence built in place are better choices. The survey notes exposure before a panel is chosen.

Panel fencing uses ready-made timber panels, usually 1.83 m wide, fixed between posts. It is quick to install and familiar in gardens and communal areas. Common panel styles include lap or waney-edge panels, closeboard-style panels, tongue-and-groove, slatted contemporary panels and decorative trellis tops.

Panel quality varies widely. Thicker boards, heavier frames and pressure treatment rather than dip treatment make a real difference to lifespan. The scope names the panel style and treatment so the quote can be compared fairly.

Panel fence repairs are usually about replacing blown or rotten panels, swapping split timber posts for concrete, or setting a leaning post upright. Where only one or two panels have failed, matching the style and colour of the remaining fence is part of the job.

Insurance claims for fence damage often need photos and a written description. iComply can provide photos of the damage and a written scope and quote to support a claim; the claim itself is between the owner and the insurer.

Repairs to panel fencing start with finding the cause. A leaning section, a broken panel or a sagging gate may come from a failed post, a loose fixing, wind damage, vehicle impact, tree roots or simple age. Fixing the cause matters, otherwise the same failure returns.

Repairs involving steel include treating any cut, drilled or welded areas with a zinc-rich primer or cold galvanising before any topcoat. Leaving bare steel exposed causes rust to spread under the remaining coating.

Storm damage often affects several bays at once. Panels blown out, posts snapped at ground level and gates wrenched off their hinges are common after high winds. Making the boundary safe comes first, followed by a permanent repair once materials are available.

Many repairs are local. Single panels, boards, pales, mesh panels, rails and fixings can usually be replaced without disturbing the rest of the line, provided matching parts are available. The repair is matched to the existing material, height and finish as closely as possible.

A repair quote sets out what has failed, why, what is being replaced and what is being left. Where the remaining parts are near the end of their life, the quote says so honestly, so the decision between repair and replacement is an informed one.

Before choosing panel fencing, it helps to write down what the boundary must achieve. Privacy, security, keeping children or animals in, marking a line, screening bins or plant, and meeting a landlord's or insurer's requirement all point to different products. A short list of priorities makes the survey quicker and the recommendation clearer.

Lifespan depends on the material and the care it gets. Timber needs treatment and will eventually need parts replaced. Galvanised and powder-coated steel lasts much longer with little maintenance. Asking what maintenance the chosen option needs, and how often, is part of choosing well.

Panels fixed to timber posts are held with galvanised brackets or screws. On concrete slotted posts, the panel simply slides down into the slots and sits on a gravel board. Lifting a panel out of slotted posts usually means removing a capping or lifting the panel clear, which needs headroom and sometimes a second person.

A concrete repair spur is a short concrete post set in the ground beside a rotten timber post and bolted to it. It saves taking the fence down and suits fences where the panels or boards are still sound. It is a repair rather than a replacement, and the scope says so.

For homes, a fence is part of the garden as much as the boundary. Height, style, colour and how it suits planting and paving matter as much as strength. A survey covers the look you want as well as the practical needs.

Neighbours share most residential boundaries. Talking to the neighbour before work starts, agreeing the line and height, and deciding which way the finished face points all help the job go smoothly.

Residents' management companies and landlords often look after shared boundaries on estates and blocks. Consistency of style across the estate, tenant access and budgets for planned work are part of the conversation.

Residential access is often tight. Materials may need carrying through a side passage or even through the house, and gardens need protecting during the work. Access is noted at the survey so the plan is realistic.

Pets and children affect the specification. Gaps under fences, gates that do not close properly and climbable rails are the usual concerns, and the scope addresses them directly.

Waste from fencing work, including old panels, posts, concrete and offcuts, is removed from site as part of the agreed scope. Where materials can be recycled, they are separated and taken to the appropriate facility.

It covers how damage is assessed, when a repair is sensible and when replacement is the better value.
fence-panels-repair.body:
When fence panels blow out or split, the fix may be a single new panel or something deeper. This page explains how damaged fence panels are replaced, how the cause is found and how the new panel is matched to the old fence.

Matching an existing fence is part of replacing panels. Styles, board thickness and colour vary between makers, so an exact match is not always possible. Where it is not, the options are a close match, a stain to blend the new panel in, or replacing a whole run so it looks consistent. The scope sets out which is planned.

Panels fixed to timber posts are held with galvanised brackets or screws. On concrete slotted posts, the panel simply slides down into the slots and sits on a gravel board. Lifting a panel out of slotted posts usually means removing a capping or lifting the panel clear, which needs headroom and sometimes a second person.

Standard panels are about 1.83 m wide, with heights commonly from around 0.9 m to 1.8 m. Older fences sometimes used other widths, so measuring the gap between posts at top and bottom matters before ordering. Where concrete slotted posts are used, the panel must also fit the slot depth.

Fence panels are the individual timber sections that make up a panel fence. Most enquiries about fence panels are about replacing one or more that have blown out, split or rotted, or about fitting new panels between posts that are still sound. The first check is always the posts, because a new panel on a failing post will not last.

A panel that blows out repeatedly is a sign of a deeper issue: posts that are loose, panels too light for the exposure or gaps that let the wind work at the fixings. Fixing the cause matters more than replacing the panel again.

Posts are the most common repair. Rotten timber posts are replaced or supported with concrete repair spurs, and leaning steel or concrete posts are reset in new foundations. Where many posts along a run have failed, replacing the run is usually better value than repairing post by post.

Vehicle damage on commercial and industrial sites tends to bend posts, rails and pales. Bent steel is replaced rather than straightened where its strength or finish has been compromised, and protection such as bollards or barriers is suggested where impacts keep happening.

Many repairs are local. Single panels, boards, pales, mesh panels, rails and fixings can usually be replaced without disturbing the rest of the line, provided matching parts are available. The repair is matched to the existing material, height and finish as closely as possible.

Storm damage often affects several bays at once. Panels blown out, posts snapped at ground level and gates wrenched off their hinges are common after high winds. Making the boundary safe comes first, followed by a permanent repair once materials are available.

Insurance claims for fence damage often need photos and a written description. iComply can provide photos of the damage and a written scope and quote to support a claim; the claim itself is between the owner and the insurer.

The old fence is taken down section by section, and old concrete footings are broken out where new posts must go in the same positions. Where old footings are too large to remove, new posts are offset and the layout is adjusted. Waste is removed and recycled where possible.

Replacement means taking down an existing fence and putting a new one up along the agreed line. It is the right choice when the posts have failed along much of the run, when the material has reached the end of its life, or when the owner wants a different type of fence.

Replacing fence panels usually follows the old line unless the owner confirms a change. Where the old fence was on a shared boundary, the owner is encouraged to agree the replacement with the neighbour first, including the height and which way the finished face points.

Neighbours and access are part of the job. Most fences can be built from one side, but finishing the far face, setting posts against an existing wall or working around planting is easier with agreed access. The finished face of a boundary fence conventionally faces outwards, and the scope records which way it is to face.

Post depth is roughly a quarter to a third of the fence height below ground, more on exposed sites or soft ground. Posts are set in concrete or compacted hardcore, depending on the system and the ground, and are plumbed in two directions and braced while the foundation sets.

Residential access is often tight. Materials may need carrying through a side passage or even through the house, and gardens need protecting during the work. Access is noted at the survey so the plan is realistic.

Neighbours share most residential boundaries. Talking to the neighbour before work starts, agreeing the line and height, and deciding which way the finished face points all help the job go smoothly.

Residents' management companies and landlords often look after shared boundaries on estates and blocks. Consistency of style across the estate, tenant access and budgets for planned work are part of the conversation.

For homes, a fence is part of the garden as much as the boundary. Height, style, colour and how it suits planting and paving matter as much as strength. A survey covers the look you want as well as the practical needs.

Pets and children affect the specification. Gaps under fences, gates that do not close properly and climbable rails are the usual concerns, and the scope addresses them directly.

Every fencing job is quoted price on application. The quote follows a survey or a review of clear photos and measurements and is based on a written scope, so you can see exactly what is included before agreeing to anything.

Waste from fencing work, including old panels, posts, concrete and offcuts, is removed from site as part of the agreed scope. Where materials can be recycled, they are separated and taken to the appropriate facility.

Work is carried out with risk assessments appropriate to the job, care around buried services and protection for lawns, paving and planting next to the line. Operatives follow site rules and inductions on commercial, school and industrial premises.

industrial-fencing.body:
Industrial fencing protects yards, plant and stock on busy, demanding sites. This page explains the heavy-duty systems used, how work is phased around operations, how buried services and hard standing are dealt with and how vehicle gates are specified.

Many industrial fences sit on boundaries with neighbouring businesses or public land. The line, height and toppings are agreed before work, and toppings are positioned so they do not overhang a neighbour's land or a public footway without agreement.

Underground services are a real risk on industrial land. Drainage, power cables, gas pipes and data ducts often run close to boundaries. Utility drawings are requested, the line is scanned with a cable avoidance tool before digging, and trial holes are dug by hand where services are suspected.

Industrial sites rarely stop for fencing work. Installation is phased around deliveries, shift patterns and yard movements, with exclusion zones around the working area and temporary barriers where a section of the old fence has to come down before the new one goes up. The sequence is agreed with the site manager in writing.

Industrial fencing protects yards, plant, stock and vehicles, and it has to survive forklifts, lorries reversing and years of weather. The usual systems are steel palisade and heavy welded mesh, with manual swing or sliding gates for vehicle access, and sometimes impact protection where vehicles turn close to the fence line.

Vehicle gates on industrial boundaries take heavy use. Manual swing gates need strong hinges, gate stops and drop bolts set into proper keeps. Sliding gates need a clear run-back area and a level track or a cantilever arrangement. Gate leaves and posts are sized for the opening, not taken from a standard list.

Ground on industrial sites is often hard standing, made ground or old foundations. Posts may need core drilling through concrete, longer posts in made ground, or base plates where digging is not possible. These decisions affect the cost and are made on site rather than assumed.

The specification for industrial fencing is usually described in a handful of terms: height, material, profile or panel type, post type and foundation, finish and colour, and gate details. When comparing quotes, checking each of those terms side by side shows whether two prices are for the same thing.

Planning rules, boundary agreements and lease terms can all affect industrial fencing. Height near a highway, conservation areas, listed buildings, planning conditions on newer estates and covenants on some properties are worth checking early. iComply flags the points it sees; the owner makes the checks and decisions.

A written scope protects both sides. It lists what is included, what is excluded, how waste is removed, how the site is left and what happens if something unexpected is found. With industrial fencing, as with most building work, the clearer the scope, the fewer disagreements at the end.

Before choosing industrial fencing, it helps to write down what the boundary must achieve. Privacy, security, keeping children or animals in, marking a line, screening bins or plant, and meeting a landlord's or insurer's requirement all point to different products. A short list of priorities makes the survey quicker and the recommendation clearer.

Lifespan depends on the material and the care it gets. Timber needs treatment and will eventually need parts replaced. Galvanised and powder-coated steel lasts much longer with little maintenance. Asking what maintenance the chosen option needs, and how often, is part of choosing well.

iComply does not publish price lists, because a headline price cannot reflect the ground, the access and the specification on your site. Every job is quoted price on application after a survey or a review of clear photos and measurements.

The cost of industrial fencing depends on a handful of factors: the length of the run, the height, the material and system, the number and type of gates, the ground conditions, access for materials and the amount of old fence to remove. Change any of those and the price changes.

Ground and access often make the biggest difference between two similar-looking jobs. Digging through tarmac, concrete, roots or made ground takes longer than digging in clear soil, and materials carried by hand through a house cost more to install than materials unloaded beside the line.

On sloping ground, steel palisade is normally raked, with the rails following the slope and the pales vertical. Where the ground changes sharply, posts may need to be longer, or a short stepped section may be used. Any gap under the bottom rail is closed down so it does not become a way in.

Perimeter fencing is a fence planned around the whole boundary of a site rather than a single run. The point is continuity: one weak section, an unfenced corner or a poorly fitted gate undoes the rest. A perimeter survey walks the full line and records every change in ground, every structure the fence meets and every opening.

Operational continuity matters. Work is phased so access for deliveries and staff is kept open, and temporary fencing is used where a section of boundary has to come down before the replacement is in place.

Industrial sites bring their own rules: inductions, permits, vehicle movement plans and restricted areas. iComply follows site rules, provides risk assessments and method statements, and agrees exclusion zones with the site manager before work starts.

Many industrial sites have security requirements set by insurers, landlords or the business itself. The fence specification is matched to those requirements, including height, profile, toppings and gate locking.

Industrial boundaries take heavy use. Vehicles turning close to the fence, stacked materials leaning against it and long years of weather all take their toll. Heavier posts, impact protection and robust gates are worth considering at specification stage.

Every fencing job is quoted price on application. The quote follows a survey or a review of clear photos and measurements and is based on a written scope, so you can see exactly what is included before agreeing to anything.

Waste from fencing work, including old panels, posts, concrete and offcuts, is removed from site as part of the agreed scope. Where materials can be recycled, they are separated and taken to the appropriate facility.

Where a specification, insurer or landlord sets requirements for a fence, the scope refers to them and the products are chosen to meet them. Certification of a product belongs to its manufacturer; iComply supplies and installs to the maker's instructions.

Work is carried out with risk assessments appropriate to the job, care around buried services and protection for lawns, paving and planting next to the line. Operatives follow site rules and inductions on commercial, school and industrial premises.

industrial-fencing-repair.body:
Industrial fences take knocks from forklifts and lorries as well as the weather. This page explains how damaged panels, pales, posts and gates are repaired on working sites and when impact protection is the better long-term answer.

Industrial sites rarely stop for fencing work. Installation is phased around deliveries, shift patterns and yard movements, with exclusion zones around the working area and temporary barriers where a section of the old fence has to come down before the new one goes up. The sequence is agreed with the site manager in writing.

Underground services are a real risk on industrial land. Drainage, power cables, gas pipes and data ducts often run close to boundaries. Utility drawings are requested, the line is scanned with a cable avoidance tool before digging, and trial holes are dug by hand where services are suspected.

Many industrial fences sit on boundaries with neighbouring businesses or public land. The line, height and toppings are agreed before work, and toppings are positioned so they do not overhang a neighbour's land or a public footway without agreement.

Vehicle gates on industrial boundaries take heavy use. Manual swing gates need strong hinges, gate stops and drop bolts set into proper keeps. Sliding gates need a clear run-back area and a level track or a cantilever arrangement. Gate leaves and posts are sized for the opening, not taken from a standard list.

Ground on industrial sites is often hard standing, made ground or old foundations. Posts may need core drilling through concrete, longer posts in made ground, or base plates where digging is not possible. These decisions affect the cost and are made on site rather than assumed.

Industrial fencing protects yards, plant, stock and vehicles, and it has to survive forklifts, lorries reversing and years of weather. The usual systems are steel palisade and heavy welded mesh, with manual swing or sliding gates for vehicle access, and sometimes impact protection where vehicles turn close to the fence line.

Storm damage often affects several bays at once. Panels blown out, posts snapped at ground level and gates wrenched off their hinges are common after high winds. Making the boundary safe comes first, followed by a permanent repair once materials are available.

Insurance claims for fence damage often need photos and a written description. iComply can provide photos of the damage and a written scope and quote to support a claim; the claim itself is between the owner and the insurer.

Many repairs are local. Single panels, boards, pales, mesh panels, rails and fixings can usually be replaced without disturbing the rest of the line, provided matching parts are available. The repair is matched to the existing material, height and finish as closely as possible.

Repairs to industrial fencing start with finding the cause. A leaning section, a broken panel or a sagging gate may come from a failed post, a loose fixing, wind damage, vehicle impact, tree roots or simple age. Fixing the cause matters, otherwise the same failure returns.

A repair quote sets out what has failed, why, what is being replaced and what is being left. Where the remaining parts are near the end of their life, the quote says so honestly, so the decision between repair and replacement is an informed one.

Installation of industrial fencing starts with setting out. The line is marked with pegs and a string line from the confirmed boundary points, corners and gate positions. Panel or bay widths are worked out from the ends so cut sections fall where they are least visible, and the post positions are marked before any digging starts.

Before digging, the line is checked for buried services using utility drawings where available and a cable avoidance tool. Where services are suspected, holes are dug by hand. Old foundations, roots and rubble found in the ground are dealt with as they are found, and any change to the plan is agreed.

Gates are hung once their posts have set firm. Hinges, latches, stops and drop bolts are fitted, and the gate is adjusted so it swings freely and closes properly. A gate that is hung on posts before the concrete has cured will often drop later.

On sloping ground, steel palisade is normally raked, with the rails following the slope and the pales vertical. Where the ground changes sharply, posts may need to be longer, or a short stepped section may be used. Any gap under the bottom rail is closed down so it does not become a way in.

Perimeter fencing is quoted for the full line with the gates, junctions, toppings and phasing included. Partial quotes for selected sections are also possible, and the scope makes clear which parts of the perimeter are included.

Industrial sites bring their own rules: inductions, permits, vehicle movement plans and restricted areas. iComply follows site rules, provides risk assessments and method statements, and agrees exclusion zones with the site manager before work starts.

Industrial boundaries take heavy use. Vehicles turning close to the fence, stacked materials leaning against it and long years of weather all take their toll. Heavier posts, impact protection and robust gates are worth considering at specification stage.

Many industrial sites have security requirements set by insurers, landlords or the business itself. The fence specification is matched to those requirements, including height, profile, toppings and gate locking.

Operational continuity matters. Work is phased so access for deliveries and staff is kept open, and temporary fencing is used where a section of boundary has to come down before the replacement is in place.

Every fencing job is quoted price on application. The quote follows a survey or a review of clear photos and measurements and is based on a written scope, so you can see exactly what is included before agreeing to anything.

Where a specification, insurer or landlord sets requirements for a fence, the scope refers to them and the products are chosen to meet them. Certification of a product belongs to its manufacturer; iComply supplies and installs to the maker's instructions.

Colours vary slightly between batches and makers, so extensions to an existing fence are matched as closely as possible and samples are checked when the match matters.

The scope identifies who instructs the work, who approves the colour and profile, and who needs to be told about access changes. Landlord consent and lease terms are the client's to check, and iComply flags where they may apply.

Pedestrian routes and accessibility shape commercial fence layouts. Gates on footpaths need a clear width, a level threshold and ironmongery that can be used easily. Fences next to public footways are kept free of sharp toppings at hand height.

Commercial fencing work is planned around opening hours. Noisy work, deliveries and areas fenced off for safety are scheduled with the site, and the working area is kept tidy and safe for staff and the public at the end of each day.

Car parks need fencing that copes with vehicles. Low kerb rails, bollards and fence lines set back from parking bays reduce damage. Where vehicles regularly clip a fence, adding protection is better value than replacing panels again and again.

Commercial fencing has to balance security with appearance. A business park, retail unit or office frontage wants a boundary that looks tidy, keeps sightlines for customers and cameras, and still deters casual intrusion. Welded mesh panel systems, railings and lower-profile palisade are the most common choices.

Posts are the most common repair. Rotten timber posts are replaced or supported with concrete repair spurs, and leaning steel or concrete posts are reset in new foundations. Where many posts along a run have failed, replacing the run is usually better value than repairing post by post.

Repairs to commercial fencing start with finding the cause. A leaning section, a broken panel or a sagging gate may come from a failed post, a loose fixing, wind damage, vehicle impact, tree roots or simple age. Fixing the cause matters, otherwise the same failure returns.

Repairs involving steel include treating any cut, drilled or welded areas with a zinc-rich primer or cold galvanising before any topcoat. Leaving bare steel exposed causes rust to spread under the remaining coating.

Insurance claims for fence damage often need photos and a written description. iComply can provide photos of the damage and a written scope and quote to support a claim; the claim itself is between the owner and the insurer.

Vehicle damage on commercial and industrial sites tends to bend posts, rails and pales. Bent steel is replaced rather than straightened where its strength or finish has been compromised, and protection such as bollards or barriers is suggested where impacts keep happening.

Storm damage often affects several bays at once. Panels blown out, posts snapped at ground level and gates wrenched off their hinges are common after high winds. Making the boundary safe comes first, followed by a permanent repair once materials are available.

Replacement means taking down an existing fence and putting a new one up along the agreed line. It is the right choice when the posts have failed along much of the run, when the material has reached the end of its life, or when the owner wants a different type of fence.

On sites where the boundary cannot be left open, replacement is phased so only a short section is down at any time, or temporary fencing is used until the new line is complete.

The old fence is taken down section by section, and old concrete footings are broken out where new posts must go in the same positions. Where old footings are too large to remove, new posts are offset and the layout is adjusted. Waste is removed and recycled where possible.

Ground clearance is a common weak point. A gap under a fence on uneven ground lets people crawl under and lets animals in. Panels are set close to the ground, and where levels change, the base is filled or the fence is stepped carefully so no large gap is left at the bottom.

Bar tops range from plain flat tops and bow tops to spear tops, ball tops and decorative finials. Bow tops and flat tops are common near play areas and schools because they have no points. Spear tops add some deterrence on frontages. The top is chosen with appearance, security and safety in mind.

Commercial boundaries are often part of a wider security plan that includes cameras, lighting, access control and alarm systems. The fence specification is coordinated with those systems so camera views are not blocked and gates suit any access control planned.

Perimeter fencing is a fence around a whole site, and its strength depends on its weakest point. This page explains how a perimeter is surveyed, how junctions and ditches are closed, and how the fence works alongside cameras and lighting.

Watercourses, culverts, ditches and drainage outlets along a boundary need careful treatment. A fence across a ditch leaves a gap underneath unless a grille or a hinged section is designed in. Any work affecting a watercourse may need consent from the relevant authority, which the owner obtains.

Perimeter fences are often combined with other security measures. Cameras, detection systems, lighting and signs work better when the fence line is straight, clear of vegetation and free of climbing aids such as bins, pallets or trees close to the fence. The survey notes climbing aids for the owner to deal with.

Perimeter fencing is a fence planned around the whole boundary of a site rather than a single run. The point is continuity: one weak section, an unfenced corner or a poorly fitted gate undoes the rest. A perimeter survey walks the full line and records every change in ground, every structure the fence meets and every opening.

Long perimeters are planned in phases. Material deliveries, the order of sections, where temporary fencing is needed and how the site stays secure overnight are set out before work starts. On larger sites, each phase is checked and signed off as it is completed.

Perimeter fencing is quoted for the full line with the gates, junctions, toppings and phasing included. Partial quotes for selected sections are also possible, and the scope makes clear which parts of the perimeter are included.

Junctions are where perimeters fail. Where a fence meets a building, a wall, a hedge or a neighbour's fence, a gap is often left. Those junctions are closed with matching panels, wing panels or toppings, and the method is written into the scope for each one.

Lifespan depends on the material and the care it gets. Timber needs treatment and will eventually need parts replaced. Galvanised and powder-coated steel lasts much longer with little maintenance. Asking what maintenance the chosen option needs, and how often, is part of choosing well.

Good access makes installation simpler. Clear routes for materials, somewhere to unload, room to work on both sides of the line and a plan for any planting or structures near the boundary all help. The survey notes access so the plan is realistic.

iComply quotes perimeter fencing price on application after a survey or after reviewing clear photos and measurements. There are no headline prices, because the cost depends on length, height, ground, access and specification, all of which differ from site to site.

Most buyers underestimate how much the ground affects the job. A level lawn, a sloping bank, a tarmac car park and a strip of made ground beside a building all need different post and foundation methods. Asking how the posts will be set, and what happens if buried services or old concrete are found, avoids surprises.

When comparing quotes, checking each of those terms side by side shows whether two prices are for the same thing.

Finishing includes fitting caps, treating any cut ends or drilled steel, checking every fixing, clearing offcuts and spoil, and leaving the ground tidy along both sides of the line. Old fencing and waste are removed from site as agreed.

Installation time depends on the length, the ground, access and the weather. The plan agreed in the scope sets out the sequence and any phasing, and the client is kept informed if conditions on the day change the plan.

Installation of perimeter fencing starts with setting out. The line is marked with pegs and a string line from the confirmed boundary points, corners and gate positions. Panel or bay widths are worked out from the ends so cut sections fall where they are least visible, and the post positions are marked before any digging starts.

Horizontal rails on the outside act like a ladder, so anti-climb designs keep rails and fixings on the inside. Panels are fitted close to the ground, and anything that could be used as a step, such as bins, walls or stacked materials next to the fence, is noted for the owner to move.

Many industrial fences sit on boundaries with neighbouring businesses or public land. The line, height and toppings are agreed before work, and toppings are positioned so they do not overhang a neighbour's land or a public footway without agreement.

Industrial boundaries take heavy use. Vehicles turning close to the fence, stacked materials leaning against it and long years of weather all take their toll. Heavier posts, impact protection and robust gates are worth considering at specification stage.

Many industrial sites have security requirements set by insurers, landlords or the business itself. The fence specification is matched to those requirements, including height, profile, toppings and gate locking.

Operational continuity matters. Work is phased so access for deliveries and staff is kept open, and temporary fencing is used where a section of boundary has to come down before the replacement is in place.

Industrial sites bring their own rules: inductions, permits, vehicle movement plans and restricted areas. iComply follows site rules, provides risk assessments and method statements, and agrees exclusion zones with the site manager before work starts.

iComply does not promise attendance or completion times in advance. Visits and installation dates are agreed directly with you, and you are kept informed if weather or ground conditions change the plan on the day.

Waste from fencing work, including old panels, posts, concrete and offcuts, is removed from site as part of the agreed scope. Where materials can be recycled, they are separated and taken to the appropriate facility.

Where a specification, insurer or landlord sets requirements for a fence, the scope refers to them and the products are chosen to meet them. Certification of a product belongs to its manufacturer; iComply supplies and installs to the maker's instructions.

Every fencing job is quoted price on application. The quote follows a survey or a review of clear photos and measurements and is based on a written scope, so you can see exactly what is included before agreeing to anything.

chain-link-fencing.body:
Chain link fencing is the economical choice for long boundaries around fields, allotments, sports areas and less sensitive land. This page explains mesh, line wires, straining posts and where chain link is and is not the right fence.

Chain link relies on tension. Straining posts at ends, corners and changes of direction carry the load of the line wires, with struts to stop them pulling over. Intermediate posts support the mesh between them. Line wires are tensioned with eye bolts or ratchets, and the mesh is tied to them at regular intervals.

Chain link fencing is woven wire mesh tensioned between posts on line wires. It is one of the most economical ways to fence a long boundary and is widely used around fields, allotments, sports areas, gardens and less sensitive commercial land. The mesh is usually galvanised or plastic coated, often in green.

A chain link fence is specified by height, mesh aperture, wire gauge and coating. Common apertures are about 50 mm, and common heights run from about 0.9 m to 2.4 m. Heavier gauge wire and a good coating resist damage and corrosion for longer.

Posts are concrete, steel angle or tubular steel. Concrete posts with strainers are common for longer runs; steel posts suit ground where concrete posts would be difficult to handle. All posts are set in concrete or compacted fill depending on the ground and the post type.

Chain link is easier to climb and cut than welded mesh, so it is not the first choice for security. Where security matters, welded mesh or palisade is suggested instead, or barbed wire strands are added at the top where suitable.

Chain link repairs include re-tensioning sagging wires, replacing damaged sections of mesh, refixing ties and resetting leaning straining posts. Where much of the mesh has rusted or the posts have failed, renewal is usually better value.

Posts are concrete, steel angle or tubular steel. Concrete posts with strainers are common for longer runs; steel posts suit ground where concrete posts would be difficult to handle. All posts are set in concrete or compacted fill depending on the ground and the post type.

Chain link fencing is woven wire mesh tensioned between posts on line wires. It is one of the most economical ways to fence a long boundary and is widely used around fields, allotments, sports areas, gardens and less sensitive commercial land. The mesh is usually galvanised or plastic coated, often in green.

Many repairs are local. Single panels, boards, pales, mesh panels, rails and fixings can usually be replaced without disturbing the rest of the line, provided matching parts are available. The repair is matched to the existing material, height and finish as closely as possible.

Insurance claims for fence damage often need photos and a written description. iComply can provide photos of the damage and a written scope and quote to support a claim; the claim itself is between the owner and the insurer.

Posts are the most common repair. Rotten timber posts are replaced or supported with concrete repair spurs, and leaning steel or concrete posts are reset in new foundations. Where many posts along a run have failed, replacing the run is usually better value than repairing post by post.

Repairs to chain link fencing start with finding the cause. A leaning section, a broken panel or a sagging gate may come from a failed post, a loose fixing, wind damage, vehicle impact, tree roots or simple age. Fixing the cause matters, otherwise the same failure returns.

Storm damage often affects several bays at once. Panels blown out, posts snapped at ground level and gates wrenched off their hinges are common after high winds. Making the boundary safe comes first, followed by a permanent repair once materials are available.

Replacement means taking down an existing fence and putting a new one up along the agreed line. It is the right choice when the posts have failed along much of the run, when the material has reached the end of its life, or when the owner wants a different type of fence.

On sites where the boundary cannot be left open, replacement is phased so only a short section is down at any time, or temporary fencing is used until the new line is complete.

Replacing chain link fencing usually follows the old line unless the owner confirms a change. Where the old fence was on a shared boundary, the owner is encouraged to agree the replacement with the neighbour first, including the height and which way the finished face points.
