A mesh fence lets people, cameras and patrols see through the boundary, which suits car parks, schools, play areas and sites with CCTV. The trade-off is that the mesh aperture and wire thickness decide how easy it is to climb or cut, so the panel is chosen for the risk.

Fence posts carry the whole fence, so when a fence leans or falls it is usually the posts that have failed. Timber posts rot at ground level, where air, water and soil meet. Concrete posts crack or snap when panels are forced or when the fence takes a heavy blow. Steel posts loosen if the foundation is too shallow or the ground is soft.

Mixed-use sites, such as flats above shops or yards behind offices, often need more than one fence type: a secure service yard, a tidy frontage and a private garden area. The scope sets out each run separately.

They give a tidy, open boundary that lasts for decades and suits frontages, apartment blocks, schools, parks, churches and civic buildings. Bar spacing, bar top, height and finish define a railing specification.

Railings are typically supplied hot-dip galvanised and polyester powder coated, often in black. On heritage frontages and in conservation areas, the style, colour and fixing method may need to match historic railings, and the owner checks any consent needed with the planning authority.

Bar tops range from plain flat tops and bow tops to spear tops, ball tops and decorative finials. Bow tops and flat tops are common near play areas and schools because they have no points. Spear tops add some deterrence on frontages. The top is chosen with appearance, security and safety in mind.

Railings can be set on posts in the ground, bolted to a dwarf wall, or leaded into a stone plinth on older properties. Each method needs a sound base. Corroded fixings into old walls are a common cause of failure, so the wall and fixings are checked before railings are refixed or replaced.

Repairs to steel railings include straightening or replacing bent bars, welding broken joints, replacing corroded sections, refixing loose panels and treating rust before repainting. Repairs on site use cold galvanising or a suitable primer on any cut or welded area before the topcoat.

Railings next to a public footway or road affect pedestrians and drivers. Work is planned so the footway stays safe, and any licence needed for working on the highway is arranged by the owner before work starts.

Most buyers underestimate how much the ground affects the job. A level lawn, a sloping bank, a tarmac car park and a strip of made ground beside a building all need different post and foundation methods. Installation time depends on the length, the ground, access and the weather. The plan agreed in the scope sets out the sequence and any phasing, and the client is kept informed if conditions on the day change the plan.

A business park, retail unit or office frontage wants a boundary that looks tidy, keeps sightlines for customers and cameras, and still deters casual intrusion. Welded mesh panel systems, railings and lower-profile palisade are the most common choices.

Ironmongery decides how well a pedestrian gate works. Self-closing hinges or closers stop gates being left open, which matters at schools and pools. Lever handles are easier to use than knobs. Locks can be keyed, coded or padlockable, and access control can be added by a specialist where needed.

Fence gates take more wear than any other part of a fence. This page explains gate posts, hinges, bracing, latches and locks for timber and steel gates, and why most gate problems are really post or hinge problems.

Timber gates are braced with a Z or diagonal brace running from the bottom hinge side up to the latch side, so the gate does not drop. A gate hung with the brace the wrong way round will sag, which is a common fault in older gates.

Hinges are chosen for the gate weight and use. Light timber gates use T-hinges or strap hinges; heavier gates use adjustable eye-and-band hinges or bolt-through hinges. Security gates use hinges that cannot be lifted off. Gate stops, drop bolts and latches finish the job.

Gate repairs include rehanging, replacing hinges, resetting posts, fitting new latches and replacing damaged boards or panels. Manual gates only are covered here; gate automation is a separate specification.

Gate posts are larger and set deeper than fence posts because they carry the weight of the gate as a lever. Timber gate posts are often 125 mm to 150 mm square, and steel gate posts are sized for the leaf width and weight. Double gates need posts on both sides set accurately so the leaves meet properly.

Fence gates are the moving part of a fence and take the most wear. Timber garden gates, steel mesh and palisade gates, railing gates and field gates all follow the same rule: the gate is only as good as the post it hangs on and the hinges that hold it. A sagging or sticking gate is usually a post or hinge problem rather than a gate problem.

Locking options range from simple thumb latches to padlockable bolts and keyed locks. Where a gate is in a security fence, the lock is positioned so it cannot be reached through the infill, and a lock guard is fitted where needed.

Planning rules, boundary agreements and lease terms can all affect fence gates. Height near a highway, conservation areas, listed buildings, planning conditions on newer estates and covenants on some properties are worth checking early. iComply flags the points it sees; the owner makes the checks and decisions.

Asking how the posts will be set, and what happens if buried services or old concrete are found, avoids surprises.

Vehicle damage on commercial and industrial sites tends to bend posts, rails and pales. Bent steel is replaced rather than straightened where its strength or finish has been compromised, and protection such as bollards or barriers is suggested where impacts keep happening.

Replacing a post means breaking out or working around the old foundation. Where the old concrete can be removed, the new post goes in the same position. Where it cannot, the new post is set alongside, which may mean adjusting the panel or rail fixings. The approach depends on what is found when the ground is opened.

Mixed-use sites, such as flats above shops or yards behind offices, often need more than one fence type: a secure service yard, a tidy frontage and a private garden area. The scope sets out each run separately.

Neighbours and access are part of the job. Most fences can be built from one side, but finishing the far face, setting posts against an existing wall or working around planting is easier with agreed access. The finished face of a boundary fence conventionally faces outwards, and the scope records which way it is to face.

Most failed fences fail at the posts. Timber posts rot at ground level, concrete posts crack where a panel has been forced, and steel posts loosen in shallow or soft foundations. Looking at the posts first tells you whether the job is a repair, a part replacement or a new line, and that decision is written down before anything is ordered.

A fence job is usually a single run along a boundary, a side return or a yard edge rather than a whole site. The questions are simple but they matter: how long is the run, how high does it need to be, what is it made of now, what condition are the posts in, and is there a gate. Answering those on site avoids ordering the wrong panels or the wrong post lengths.

Replacing a fence on the same line is the most common job. The old panels, boards and posts are taken down, the old concrete is broken out or new holes are set alongside it, and the new posts are set plumb and in line. Gravel boards keep timber off the soil and are worth including on almost every timber fence.

Posts are set to the depth and foundation the system and the ground require. They are set plumb in both directions and in line, and braced while concrete cures. Getting the posts right is most of the job, because everything else hangs from them.

Before digging, the line is checked for buried services using utility drawings where available and a cable avoidance tool. Where services are suspected, holes are dug by hand. Old foundations, roots and rubble found in the ground are dealt with as they are found, and any change to the plan is agreed.

At handover, the work is walked with the client, gates are demonstrated, and any maintenance needs are explained, such as treating timber or keeping vegetation clear of mesh. Product details and any manufacturer information are passed on.

Gates are hung once their posts have set firm. Hinges, latches, stops and drop bolts are fitted, and the gate is adjusted so it swings freely and closes properly. A gate that is hung on posts before the concrete has cured will often drop later.

Panel or bay widths are worked out from the ends so cut sections fall where they are least visible, and the post positions are marked before any digging starts.

Shared boundaries are common in terraced and semi-detached housing. Agreeing the line, the height and the finished face with the neighbour before work starts avoids disputes later. The owner makes that agreement; iComply fences to the line it is given.

Mixed-use sites, such as flats above shops or yards behind offices, often need more than one fence type: a secure service yard, a tidy frontage and a private garden area. The scope sets out each run separately.

Where a specification, insurer or landlord sets requirements for a fence, the scope refers to them and the products are chosen to meet them. Certification of a product belongs to its manufacturer; iComply supplies and installs to the maker's instructions.

fencing-contractors.intro: This guide to Fencing Contractors explains boundary, security and garden fencing chosen from a measured site survey, what decides the right approach for facilities managers, business owners, landlords and managing agents, and how iComply scopes the work before anything is ordered. It sets out what to expect from a fencing contractor, how iComply scopes, manages and finishes work, and how to compare quotes fairly.
fencing-contractors.body:
Choosing fencing contractors is mainly about clarity and workmanship. This page explains what a good contractor should provide, how iComply surveys and scopes fencing work, and how to compare quotes on the same facts.

Finish and maintenance are part of the choice. Pressure-treated timber still benefits from a preservative or stain every few years. Galvanised steel resists corrosion for a long time, and a powder-coated finish over galvanising adds colour and a further barrier. Cut ends, drilled holes and damaged coating are treated on site so corrosion does not start where the fence was altered.

A written fencing scope lists the run lengths, the height, the product family and profile, the post type and foundation, the gate positions and hardware, the finish, what happens to any old fence and how the site is left. That document is what the price on application is based on, so two quotes can be compared on the same facts.

Height is a planning question as well as a practical one. Many boundary fences can be put up without an application, but limits apply next to highways and on some frontages, and listed buildings, conservation areas and planning conditions can change the position. iComply flags where a height or position may need a check with the local planning authority; the decision belongs to the owner and the authority.

Boundary lines are confirmed by the owner before a post goes in. Where a fence replaces an older one, the new line normally follows the old post positions unless the owner says otherwise. Where neighbours share a boundary, the owner is encouraged to agree the line and the finished face first. iComply fences the line it is shown and does not decide a legal boundary.

Ground conditions drive more of the cost and the lifespan than most people expect. Clay, made ground, tree roots, buried services, slopes and hard surfaces all change how posts are set. Posts are concreted, driven or base-plated to suit what is found when the line is walked, and a trial hole is dug where the ground is unknown rather than guessing a foundation depth.

Choosing a contractor for fencing is mostly about clarity and workmanship. A good contractor surveys before quoting, writes a scope that lists what is included, explains the specification in plain terms and tells you what happens if something unexpected is found in the ground.

After installation, a contractor should be easy to contact for adjustments. Gates settle, fixings may need tightening and timber moves in its first season. iComply returns by arrangement to put right any issues with its own workmanship.

Insurance, risk assessments and method statements are normal for commercial and school work. iComply provides the documents the site requires, follows site rules and inductions, and works to the agreed hours.

iComply Property Services is a property maintenance and installation business based in Stockport. It carries out fencing for homes, landlords, managing agents, schools, commercial and industrial sites across Greater Manchester and the surrounding towns, with work quoted price on application.

Comparing quotes is easier when each one names the same things: length, height, product, post type, foundation, finish, gates, waste removal and making good. A low price that leaves out posts, gravel boards or removal is not a like-for-like comparison.

Gates are hung once their posts have set firm. Hinges, latches, stops and drop bolts are fitted, and the gate is adjusted so it swings freely and closes properly. A gate that is hung on posts before the concrete has cured will often drop later.

Installation time depends on the length, the ground, access and the weather. The plan agreed in the scope sets out the sequence and any phasing, and the client is kept informed if conditions on the day change the plan.

Before digging, the line is checked for buried services using utility drawings where available and a cable avoidance tool. Where services are suspected, holes are dug by hand. Old foundations, roots and rubble found in the ground are dealt with as they are found, and any change to the plan is agreed.

Palisade fencing is made of vertical steel pales bolted to horizontal rails, which are fixed to steel posts set in concrete. It is one of the most common commercial and industrial boundaries in the UK because it is strong, familiar and hard to climb without tools. The specification is described by pale profile, pale top, height and finish.

Some specifications ask for products certified to a recognised security standard, such as LPS 1175 or Secured by Design. Where a specification calls for that, iComply supplies and fits the certified product to the manufacturer's installation instructions. iComply does not certify fences itself, and a certification belongs to the product as tested, not to the installer.

Many commercial premises are leased. Tenants should check lease terms and landlord consent before changing a boundary, and managing agents often want a written specification for approval. The scope is written to support that process.

Commercial boundaries are often part of a wider security plan that includes cameras, lighting, access control and alarm systems. The fence specification is coordinated with those systems so camera views are not blocked and gates suit any access control planned.

Commercial customers often need documents for their own records: insurance details, risk assessments, method statements and product information. Those are provided as part of the job.

Facilities managers need fencing work that fits around the business. Out-of-hours working, phased installation, clear method statements and a tidy site at the end of each day are normal requirements and are agreed before work starts.

Insurers sometimes ask for specific security measures as a condition of cover. Where an insurer or security consultant has set a requirement, the fence is specified to meet it, and the scope refers to the requirement.

iComply Property Services works from a workshop at 17 Woodlands Park Road, Offerton, Stockport, Cheshire SK2 5DE. Fencing enquiries can be sent by phone or WhatsApp on 07517 806082, or by email to info@icomplypropertyservices.co.uk, with the site address, a few photos and a rough idea of the length and height.

Work is carried out with risk assessments appropriate to the job, care around buried services and protection for lawns, paving and planting next to the line. Operatives follow site rules and inductions on commercial, school and industrial premises.

Every fencing job is quoted price on application. The quote follows a survey or a review of clear photos and measurements and is based on a written scope, so you can see exactly what is included before agreeing to anything.

Where a specification, insurer or landlord sets requirements for a fence, the scope refers to them and the products are chosen to meet them. Certification of a product belongs to its manufacturer; iComply supplies and installs to the maker's instructions.

How long does fencing last?

It depends on the material, the finish, the ground and the exposure. Treated timber lasts longer with regular preservative, and galvanised or powder-coated steel lasts far longer than bare steel. The scope states the finish so expectations are clear.

fencing-installers.body:
Fencing installers make the difference between a fence that stands straight for years and one that leans within a season. This page explains what experienced installers pay attention to, from post depth to gate hanging.

Replacing a fence on the same line is the most common job. The old panels, boards and posts are taken down, the old concrete is broken out or new holes are set alongside it, and the new posts are set plumb and in line. Gravel boards keep timber off the soil and are worth including on almost every timber fence.

Most failed fences fail at the posts. Timber posts rot at ground level, concrete posts crack where a panel has been forced, and steel posts loosen in shallow or soft foundations. Looking at the posts first tells you whether the job is a repair, a part replacement or a new line, and that decision is written down before anything is ordered.

Slopes need a decision before work starts. Panels and mesh can be stepped down a slope, which leaves triangular gaps at the bottom that are filled with gravel boards, or the fence can be raked to follow the ground, which suits closeboard and some mesh systems. Which is right depends on the look you want and what the fence must keep in or out.

A fence is quoted after a visit or from clear photos with measurements. The written scope gives the run length, height, product, post type, gate details and how waste is taken away, and the price is on application once that scope is agreed.

A fence job is usually a single run along a boundary, a side return or a yard edge rather than a whole site. The questions are simple but they matter: how long is the run, how high does it need to be, what is it made of now, what condition are the posts in, and is there a gate. Answering those on site avoids ordering the wrong panels or the wrong post lengths.

iComply Property Services is a property maintenance and installation business based in Stockport. It carries out fencing for homes, landlords, managing agents, schools, commercial and industrial sites across Greater Manchester and the surrounding towns, with work quoted price on application.

Replacement means taking down an existing fence and putting a new one up along the agreed line. It is the right choice when the posts have failed along much of the run, when the material has reached the end of its life, or when the owner wants a different type of fence.

Replacement is a good time to reconsider the specification. Concrete posts and gravel boards instead of timber, a heavier panel for an exposed garden, mesh instead of palisade for better visibility, or a different height can all be considered while the line is open.

Replacing fence usually follows the old line unless the owner confirms a change. Where the old fence was on a shared boundary, the owner is encouraged to agree the replacement with the neighbour first, including the height and which way the finished face points.

Because it is built board by board, closeboard follows the ground. On a slope the rails can be raked so the top of the fence runs parallel to the ground, with no stepped gaps underneath. Run lengths do not have to match a panel width, which helps on awkward boundaries, corners and short returns.

A concrete repair spur is a short concrete post set in the ground beside a rotten timber post and bolted to it. It saves taking the fence down and suits fences where the panels or boards are still sound. It is a repair rather than a replacement, and the scope says so.

Shared boundaries are common in terraced and semi-detached housing. Agreeing the line, the height and the finished face with the neighbour before work starts avoids disputes later. The owner makes that agreement; iComply fences to the line it is given.

Homeowners usually want a fence that looks good, gives privacy and lasts. Landlords and managing agents want something durable and easy to maintain across several properties. Businesses want security and a tidy frontage. The same survey approach works for all of them, with the specification adjusted to suit.

Mixed-use sites, such as flats above shops or yards behind offices, often need more than one fence type: a secure service yard, a tidy frontage and a private garden area. The scope sets out each run separately.

Landlords and agents often need fencing work coordinated with tenants. Access dates, keys, pets and parking are agreed in advance, and photos of the finished work can be supplied for the property file.

Waste from fencing work, including old panels, posts, concrete and offcuts, is removed from site as part of the agreed scope. Where materials can be recycled, they are separated and taken to the appropriate facility.

Where a specification, insurer or landlord sets requirements for a fence, the scope refers to them and the products are chosen to meet them. Certification of a product belongs to its manufacturer; iComply supplies and installs to the maker's instructions.

Can you replace just part of a fence?
Yes, where the remaining posts and panels are sound. If most posts have rotted or loosened, a new line is usually the better value, and the scope explains why.

Conventionally the finished face of a boundary fence faces outwards, towards the neighbour or the road, with the posts and rails on the owner's side. The scope records the agreed direction.

fencing-quote.intro: Fencing Quote: a single fence line put up, put right or replaced to the boundary you confirm. iComply works for homeowners, landlords and residents' management companies from its Stockport workshop, measures before it specifies, and quotes every job price on application. It explains what drives the cost of fence, why quotes are price on application, and how to get an accurate written quote.
fencing-quote.body:
Getting a fencing quote is quicker when you know what to send. This page explains the information that helps, how a survey or photos lead to a written scope, and what a good quote should include so it can be compared fairly.

Replacing a fence on the same line is the most common job. The old panels, boards and posts are taken down, the old concrete is broken out or new holes are set alongside it, and the new posts are set plumb and in line. Gravel boards keep timber off the soil and are worth including on almost every timber fence.

A fence job is usually a single run along a boundary, a side return or a yard edge rather than a whole site. The questions are simple but they matter: how long is the run, how high does it need to be, what is it made of now, what condition are the posts in, and is there a gate. Answering those on site avoids ordering the wrong panels or the wrong post lengths.

Most failed fences fail at the posts. Timber posts rot at ground level, concrete posts crack where a panel has been forced, and steel posts loosen in shallow or soft foundations. Looking at the posts first tells you whether the job is a repair, a part replacement or a new line, and that decision is written down before anything is ordered.

Neighbours and access are part of the job. Most fences can be built from one side, but finishing the far face, setting posts against an existing wall or working around planting is easier with agreed access. The finished face of a boundary fence conventionally faces outwards, and the scope records which way it is to face.

Slopes need a decision before work starts. Panels and mesh can be stepped down a slope, which leaves triangular gaps at the bottom that are filled with gravel boards, or the fence can be raked to follow the ground, which suits closeboard and some mesh systems. Which is right depends on the look you want and what the fence must keep in or out.

Specification choices change both the upfront cost and the lifetime cost. Concrete posts cost more than timber at the start but rarely need replacing. Powder-coated steel costs more than bare galvanised but looks better for longer. A quote that explains those trade-offs helps you choose.

iComply does not publish price lists, because a headline price cannot reflect the ground, the access and the specification on your site. Every job is quoted price on application after a survey or a review of clear photos and measurements.

Ground and access often make the biggest difference between two similar-looking jobs. Digging through tarmac, concrete, roots or made ground takes longer than digging in clear soil, and materials carried by hand through a house cost more to install than materials unloaded beside the line.

To get an accurate quote quickly, send the address, the approximate length and height, photos of the boundary and any gates, and a note of what you want the fence to achieve. A written scope and quote follow, listing what is included.

The cost of fence depends on a handful of factors: the length of the run, the height, the material and system, the number and type of gates, the ground conditions, access for materials and the amount of old fence to remove. Change any of those and the price changes.

Local planning authorities across Greater Manchester and the surrounding boroughs apply the same national rules on fence heights, but conservation areas, listed buildings and estate conditions differ. iComply flags where a local check may be needed, and the owner contacts the authority.

A local contractor is easy to reach after the job too. If something needs adjusting once the new work has settled in, such as a gate that needs rehanging or a fixing that needs tightening, the same team that installed it can come back by arrangement.

Searching for fence near you usually means wanting someone who knows local conditions. Across Greater Manchester, clay soils, Pennine exposure on the eastern edges, older terraces with shared boundaries and large industrial estates all shape how fencing is specified and installed.

Panel fences on slopes are stepped, with each panel level and the posts set at different heights. The triangular gaps below are filled with gravel boards cut to suit. That stepped look suits some gardens and not others, and the alternative of a raked closeboard fence is mentioned where it fits better.

Fence posts carry the whole fence, so when a fence leans or falls it is usually the posts that have failed. Timber posts rot at ground level, where air, water and soil meet. Concrete posts crack or snap when panels are forced or when the fence takes a heavy blow. Steel posts loosen if the foundation is too shallow or the ground is soft.

Residential access is often tight. Materials may need carrying through a side passage or even through the house, and gardens need protecting during the work. Access is noted at the survey so the plan is realistic.

Neighbours share most residential boundaries. Talking to the neighbour before work starts, agreeing the line and height, and deciding which way the finished face points all help the job go smoothly.

For homes, a fence is part of the garden as much as the boundary. Height, style, colour and how it suits planting and paving matter as much as strength. A survey covers the look you want as well as the practical needs.

Pets and children affect the specification. Gaps under fences, gates that do not close properly and climbable rails are the usual concerns, and the scope addresses them directly.

Residents' management companies and landlords often look after shared boundaries on estates and blocks. Consistency of style across the estate, tenant access and budgets for planned work are part of the conversation.

Work is carried out with risk assessments appropriate to the job, care around buried services and protection for lawns, paving and planting next to the line. Operatives follow site rules and inductions on commercial, school and industrial premises.

Where a specification, insurer or landlord sets requirements for a fence, the scope refers to them and the products are chosen to meet them. Certification of a product belongs to its manufacturer; iComply supplies and installs to the maker's instructions.

iComply does not promise attendance or completion times in advance. Visits and installation dates are agreed directly with you, and you are kept informed if weather or ground conditions change the plan on the day.

iComply Property Services works from a workshop at 17 Woodlands Park Road, Offerton, Stockport, Cheshire SK2 5DE. Fencing enquiries can be sent by phone or WhatsApp on 07517 806082, or by email to info@icomplypropertyservices.co.uk, with the site address, a few photos and a rough idea of the length and height.
focus_points: Run length, height and post condition recorded first
Repair, part replacement or new line decided in writing
Gravel boards, stepping or raking agreed for slopes
Finished face and access agreed before work starts
Price on application
faq: Which way should the fence face?
Conventionally the finished face of a boundary fence faces outwards, towards the neighbour or the road, with the posts and rails on the owner's side. The scope records the agreed direction.
What happens to the old fence?
It is taken down and removed from site unless you ask to keep any part of it. Removal is written into the scope.
How much does fencing cost?
It depends on length, height, material, gates, ground, access and removal of any old fence. Every job is quoted price on application from a written scope.
Can you quote from photos?
Often, if the photos are clear and include measurements. Some sites need a survey visit first.
Do I need my neighbour's permission?
For a fence on your own land, usually not, but agreeing the line and finished face with your neighbour avoids disputes. Shared boundaries need agreement.
How do I ask for a quote for Fencing Quote?

Phone or WhatsApp 07517 806082, or email info@icomplypropertyservices.co.uk, with the site address, photos and what you need. The reply is price on application once the scope is written. Workshop: 17 Woodlands Park Road, Offerton, Stockport, Cheshire SK2 5DE.

fence-posts-replacement.seo_title: Fence Posts Replacement | iComply Property Services

fence-posts-replacement.body:
Fence posts replacement is often the answer when a fence leans or falls. This page explains how failed posts are diagnosed, how old foundations are dealt with and when concrete posts or repair spurs are the right choice.

Replacing a post means breaking out or working around the old foundation. Where the old concrete can be removed, the new post goes in the same position. Where it cannot, the new post is set alongside, which may mean adjusting the panel or rail fixings. The approach depends on what is found when the ground is opened.

Fence posts carry the whole fence, so when a fence leans or falls it is usually the posts that have failed. Timber posts rot at ground level, where air, water and soil meet. Concrete posts crack or snap when panels are forced or when the fence takes a heavy blow. Steel posts loosen if the foundation is too shallow or the ground is soft.

A concrete repair spur is a short concrete post set in the ground beside a rotten timber post and bolted to it. It saves taking the fence down and suits fences where the panels or boards are still sound. It is a repair rather than a replacement, and the scope says so.

Steel posts for mesh and palisade systems follow the manufacturer's size, spacing and foundation guidance. Base-plated posts are bolted to existing concrete or slabs where digging is not possible, using fixings chosen for the base, and are only used where the base can take the load.

Concrete fence posts are a long-lasting replacement for timber in panel fences. Slotted concrete posts hold panels in grooves, and mortice posts take arris rails for closeboard. Both are heavy and need careful handling and setting, but they do not rot, and they are the usual choice when timber posts have already failed once.

The old fence is taken down section by section, and old concrete footings are broken out where new posts must go in the same positions. Where old footings are too large to remove, new posts are offset and the layout is adjusted. Waste is removed and recycled where possible.

Replacement is a good time to reconsider the specification. Concrete posts and gravel boards instead of timber, a heavier panel for an exposed garden, mesh instead of palisade for better visibility, or a different height can all be considered while the line is open.

On sites where the boundary cannot be left open, replacement is phased so only a short section is down at any time, or temporary fencing is used until the new line is complete.

Replacing fence posts usually follows the old line unless the owner confirms a change. Where the old fence was on a shared boundary, the owner is encouraged to agree the replacement with the neighbour first, including the height and which way the finished face points.

Replacement means taking down an existing fence and putting a new one up along the agreed line. It is the right choice when the posts have failed along much of the run, when the material has reached the end of its life, or when the owner wants a different type of fence.

Many repairs are local. Single panels, boards, pales, mesh panels, rails and fixings can usually be replaced without disturbing the rest of the line, provided matching parts are available. The repair is matched to the existing material, height and finish as closely as possible.

Vehicle damage on commercial and industrial sites tends to bend posts, rails and pales. Bent steel is replaced rather than straightened where its strength or finish has been compromised, and protection such as bollards or barriers is suggested where impacts keep happening.

A repair quote sets out what has failed, why, what is being replaced and what is being left. Where the remaining parts are near the end of their life, the quote says so honestly, so the decision between repair and replacement is an informed one.

Panels are fixed either to timber posts with brackets or screws, or slotted into the grooves of concrete posts. Concrete slotted posts with concrete gravel boards are the most durable option at ground level, because nothing timber touches the soil, and panels can be lifted out and replaced without disturbing the posts.

Closeboard repairs are often possible without taking the fence down. Broken arris rails can be strengthened with galvanised repair brackets or replaced, split boards can be swapped one at a time, and rotten gravel boards replaced. Where the posts themselves have rotted, setting new posts or concrete spurs is usually the lasting answer.

Pets and children affect the specification. Gaps under fences, gates that do not close properly and climbable rails are the usual concerns, and the scope addresses them directly.

Neighbours share most residential boundaries. Talking to the neighbour before work starts, agreeing the line and height, and deciding which way the finished face points all help the job go smoothly.

For homes, a fence is part of the garden as much as the boundary. Height, style, colour and how it suits planting and paving matter as much as strength. A survey covers the look you want as well as the practical needs.

Residents' management companies and landlords often look after shared boundaries on estates and blocks. Consistency of style across the estate, tenant access and budgets for planned work are part of the conversation.

Residential access is often tight. Materials may need carrying through a side passage or even through the house, and gardens need protecting during the work. Access is noted at the survey so the plan is realistic.

iComply Property Services works from a workshop at 17 Woodlands Park Road, Offerton, Stockport, Cheshire SK2 5DE. Fencing enquiries can be sent by phone or WhatsApp on 07517 806082, or by email to info@icomplypropertyservices.co.uk, with the site address, a few photos and a rough idea of the length and height.

Waste from fencing work, including old panels, posts, concrete and offcuts, is removed from site as part of the agreed scope. Where materials can be recycled, they are separated and taken to the appropriate facility.

iComply does not promise attendance or completion times in advance. Visits and installation dates are agreed directly with you, and you are kept informed if weather or ground conditions change the plan on the day.

Every fencing job is quoted price on application. The quote follows a survey or a review of clear photos and measurements and is based on a written scope, so you can see exactly what is included before agreeing to anything.

faq: Will the new fence go on the same line?
Yes, unless you confirm a change. On shared boundaries, we recommend agreeing the line and finished face with the neighbour first.
Can the boundary stay secure during replacement?
Yes. Work can be phased, or temporary fencing used, so the site is not left open.
Do I need my neighbour's permission?
For a fence on your own land, usually not, but agreeing the line and finished face with your neighbour avoids disputes. Shared boundaries need agreement.
Can you replace fence posts without replacing the fence?
Often, yes. Panels or rails are taken off, the post replaced, and the fence refitted. Where many posts have failed, a new fence may be better value.
Are concrete fence posts better than timber?
They last much longer at ground level because they do not rot. They are heavier to handle but are the usual replacement when timber posts have failed.

Old foundations, roots and rubble found in the ground are dealt with as they are found, and any change to the plan is agreed.

Installation time depends on the length, the ground, access and the weather. The plan agreed in the scope sets out the sequence and any phasing, and the client is kept informed if conditions on the day change the plan.

Finishing includes fitting caps, treating any cut ends or drilled steel, checking every fixing, clearing offcuts and spoil, and leaving the ground tidy along both sides of the line. Old fencing and waste are removed from site as agreed.

Gates are hung once their posts have set firm. Hinges, latches, stops and drop bolts are fitted, and the gate is adjusted so it swings freely and closes properly. A gate that is hung on posts before the concrete has cured will often drop later.

Installation of fence posts starts with setting out. The line is marked with pegs and a string line from the confirmed boundary points, corners and gate positions. temporary-fencing-hire.seo_title: Temporary Fencing Hire | iComply Property Services

temporary-fencing-hire.intro: Temporary Fencing Hire from iComply Property Services covers mesh panels on weighted feet, clamped and braced for sites, events and short-term security. This guide is written for principal contractors, developers, site managers and event organisers and starts from a site survey and a written scope, not a catalogue price. It covers how temporary fence hire is scoped: the layout, the period, delivery and collection, bracing and responsibility for checks.
temporary-fencing-hire.body:
Temporary fencing hire covers supply, installation, changes during the hire and collection. This page explains how the layout, period, bracing and inspection responsibilities are agreed for sites and events.

Clamps should be fitted so they cannot easily be undone from outside, and anti-lift clips can stop panels being lifted out of their feet. On sites where security matters, the clamp positions and bracing are set inside the fenced area.

Temporary fencing on or next to the highway needs care. Fences on public footways may need a licence from the highway authority, and pedestrian routes have to stay safe and accessible. The site owner or principal contractor arranges any licence; iComply installs to the agreed layout.

Temporary fencing is made of free-standing mesh panels, typically about 3.5 m long and 2.0 m high, set in heavy rubber or concrete feet and joined with couplers or clamps. It is used to secure building sites, separate the public from works, close off areas during repairs and control crowds at events.

Temporary fencing needs checking while it is up. Panels get moved, clamps disappear and feet are knocked out of line. Regular inspection, especially after high winds, keeps the line continuous and stable. The scope says who carries out those checks.

Temporary fencing can be supplied for a set period, moved as a site changes, and taken away at the end. The scope records the line, the length, the period, the gates and any covering, and the price is on application.

Stability is the key point. Temporary panels catch the wind, especially when covered with debris netting, banners or shade cloth. Bracing stays and extra weights are added at intervals and at ends and corners, and covered panels need more bracing than bare mesh. The layout is planned with exposure and any cladding in mind.

During the hire, someone needs to check the fence regularly, especially after high winds or when the site layout changes. The hire scope makes clear whether iComply carries out those checks or whether the site team does.

Temporary fencing hire covers supply, installation, any changes to the layout during the hire period, and collection at the end. The scope records the length, number of panels, feet, couplers, bracing, gates and any covering, along with the delivery address and the start and end dates.

Hire is quoted price on application. The price depends on the quantity, the period, delivery distance, installation, any changes during the period and collection.

Hire periods range from a single event to many months on a construction site. Longer hires often involve moving sections as the work progresses, adding gates or extending the line, and those changes are agreed and recorded as they happen.

Lost or damaged panels, feet and clamps are a common issue with temporary fencing. The scope sets out how missing or damaged items are handled so there are no surprises at collection.

A local contractor is easy to reach after the job too. If something needs adjusting once the new work has settled in, such as a gate that needs rehanging or a fixing that needs tightening, the same team that installed it can come back by arrangement.

Local planning authorities across Greater Manchester and the surrounding boroughs apply the same national rules on fence heights, but conservation areas, listed buildings and estate conditions differ. iComply flags where a local check may be needed, and the owner contacts the authority.

Searching for temporary fencing near you usually means wanting someone who knows local conditions. Across Greater Manchester, clay soils, Pennine exposure on the eastern edges, older terraces with shared boundaries and large industrial estates all shape how fencing is specified and installed.

Visibility is one of the main reasons to choose mesh over palisade. A mesh fence lets people, cameras and patrols see through the boundary, which suits car parks, schools, play areas and sites with CCTV. The trade-off is that the mesh aperture and wire thickness decide how easy it is to climb or cut, so the panel is chosen for the risk.

Timber gates are braced with a Z or diagonal brace running from the bottom hinge side up to the latch side, so the gate does not drop. A gate hung with the brace the wrong way round will sag, which is a common fault in older gates.

Construction sites need boundaries that change as the work progresses. Temporary fencing and hoarding are moved, extended and adapted as phases change, and those changes are agreed with the site manager.

Principal contractors set site rules, inductions and permits. iComply follows them, provides risk assessments and method statements, and works within the site's logistics plan for deliveries and access.

At the end of a project, temporary boundaries are removed and the ground reinstated as agreed. Where permanent fencing follows, the change from temporary to permanent is sequenced so the site is never left open.

Licences for fencing or hoarding on the highway are arranged by the site owner or principal contractor. iComply installs to the licensed layout and keeps pedestrian routes safe.

Every fencing job is quoted price on application. The quote follows a survey or a review of clear photos and measurements and is based on a written scope, so you can see exactly what is included before agreeing to anything.

Work is carried out with risk assessments appropriate to the job, care around buried services and protection for lawns, paving and planting next to the line. Operatives follow site rules and inductions on commercial, school and industrial premises.

iComply does not promise attendance or completion times in advance. Visits and installation dates are agreed directly with you, and you are kept informed if weather or ground conditions change the plan on the day.

Typical panels are about 3.5 m long and 2.0 m high, set in rubber or concrete feet and joined with couplers.
Does temporary fencing blow over?
It can if it is not braced and weighted properly, especially when covered with netting or banners. Bracing and extra weights are added for exposure.
Do I need a licence for fencing on the pavement?
Often, yes. The site owner or principal contractor arranges any highway licence before the fence goes up.
How long can I hire temporary fencing for?
From a single event to many months. Changes to the layout during the hire can be arranged.
Who checks the fence during the hire?
The scope states whether iComply or your site team carries out regular checks.

site-hoarding-installation.body:
Site hoarding installation creates a solid, stable screen around a construction or refurbishment site. This page explains timber and panel hoarding, bracing for wind, gates, licences and graphics.

At the end of a project, hoarding is dismantled, materials removed and the ground reinstated as agreed. Where hoarding has been fixed to existing surfaces, making good is written into the scope from the start.

Hoarding next to a public footway or road usually needs a licence from the highway authority, and conditions may apply to lighting, walkway widths, corners and visibility at junctions. The licence and its conditions are arranged by the site owner or principal contractor before installation.

Plywood hoarding is usually painted to a specified colour, with graphics or signs fixed afterwards. Panels are inspected regularly for damage, graffiti and loosened fixings, and repairs are made to keep the line safe and tidy.

Gates in hoarding need careful design. Personnel and vehicle gates must open without swinging into the footway, lock securely and be wide enough for deliveries. Viewing panels, lighting points and spaces for graphics are planned into the layout rather than cut in later.

Site hoarding is a solid screen around a construction or refurbishment site. It keeps the public out, hides the works, reduces dust and noise reaching the street and gives space for signs and graphics. Common types are timber-framed plywood hoarding, steel-framed panel systems and solid infill panels fitted to temporary fence bases.

Hoarding is solid, so wind load is much higher than for mesh fencing. Timber hoarding needs posts set in the ground or properly weighted bases, raking props or bracing at suitable spacing, and a design that suits the height and exposure. Taller or exposed hoardings may need an engineered design, which the principal contractor provides or commissions.

Posts are set to the depth and foundation the system and the ground require. They are set plumb in both directions and in line, and braced while concrete cures. Getting the posts right is most of the job, because everything else hangs from them.

Installation of site hoarding starts with setting out. The line is marked with pegs and a string line from the confirmed boundary points, corners and gate positions. Panel or bay widths are worked out from the ends so cut sections fall where they are least visible, and the post positions are marked before any digging starts.

At handover, the work is walked with the client, gates are demonstrated, and any maintenance needs are explained, such as treating timber or keeping vegetation clear of mesh. Product details and any manufacturer information are passed on.

Gates are hung once their posts have set firm. Hinges, latches, stops and drop bolts are fitted, and the gate is adjusted so it swings freely and closes properly. A gate that is hung on posts before the concrete has cured will often drop later.

Once the posts are set, rails, panels, boards, pales or mesh are fixed in order along the run. Levels are checked as the work progresses so the top line is consistent, and adjustments are made for slopes by stepping or raking as agreed in the scope.

Photos help a local enquiry move quickly. A few photos of the boundary, a rough measurement of the length and height, and a note of any gates, slopes or access issues mean the first conversation can be specific. Send them by WhatsApp or email, and a survey can be arranged if one is needed.

Local work keeps travel and delivery simple. Materials are ordered for the job once the scope is agreed and delivered to site or collected from local suppliers. Waste is taken away rather than left in a skip on the street unless a skip has been agreed.

Local planning authorities across Greater Manchester and the surrounding boroughs apply the same national rules on fence heights, but conservation areas, listed buildings and estate conditions differ. iComply flags where a local check may be needed, and the owner contacts the authority.

Gate posts are larger and set deeper than fence posts because they carry the weight of the gate as a lever. Timber gate posts are often 125 mm to 150 mm square, and steel gate posts are sized for the leaf width and weight. Double gates need posts on both sides set accurately so the leaves meet properly.

Commercial fencing work is planned around opening hours. Noisy work, deliveries and areas fenced off for safety are scheduled with the site, and the working area is kept tidy and safe for staff and the public at the end of each day.

Principal contractors set site rules, inductions and permits. iComply follows them, provides risk assessments and method statements, and works within the site's logistics plan for deliveries and access.

At the end of a project, temporary boundaries are removed and the ground reinstated as agreed. Where permanent fencing follows, the change from temporary to permanent is sequenced so the site is never left open.

Licences for fencing or hoarding on the highway are arranged by the site owner or principal contractor. iComply installs to the licensed layout and keeps pedestrian routes safe.

Construction sites need boundaries that change as the work progresses. Temporary fencing and hoarding are moved, extended and adapted as phases change, and those changes are agreed with the site manager.

Waste from fencing work, including old panels, posts, concrete and offcuts, is removed from site as part of the agreed scope. Where materials can be recycled, they are separated and taken to the appropriate facility.

fallen-fence-repair.intro: Fallen Fence Repair from iComply Property Services covers a single fence line put up, put right or replaced to the boundary you confirm. This guide is written for homeowners, landlords, managing agents and businesses and starts from a site survey and a written scope, not a catalogue price. It explains how a fallen or storm-damaged fence is made safe and then repaired properly, without promising attendance times.
fallen-fence-repair.body:
A fallen fence needs making safe first and repairing properly second. This page explains how a fallen or storm-damaged fence is secured, how the cause of the failure is found and how a lasting repair is made, without promising attendance times.

A fence is quoted after a visit or from clear photos with measurements. The written scope gives the run length, height, product, post type, gate details and how waste is taken away, and the price is on application once that scope is agreed.

Replacing a fence on the same line is the most common job. The old panels, boards and posts are taken down, the old concrete is broken out or new holes are set alongside it, and the new posts are set plumb and in line. Gravel boards keep timber off the soil and are worth including on almost every timber fence.

Neighbours and access are part of the job. Most fences can be built from one side, but finishing the far face, setting posts against an existing wall or working around planting is easier with agreed access. The finished face of a boundary fence conventionally faces outwards, and the scope records which way it is to face.

Slopes need a decision before work starts. Panels and mesh can be stepped down a slope, which leaves triangular gaps at the bottom that are filled with gravel boards, or the fence can be raked to follow the ground, which suits closeboard and some mesh systems. Which is right depends on the look you want and what the fence must keep in or out.

A fence job is usually a single run along a boundary, a side return or a yard edge rather than a whole site. The questions are simple but they matter: how long is the run, how high does it need to be, what is it made of now, what condition are the posts in, and is there a gate. Answering those on site avoids ordering the wrong panels or the wrong post lengths.

The permanent repair may be new posts, replacement panels, a part replacement or a new run, depending on what is found. Photos of the damage taken at the time help both the repair quote and any insurance claim.

A fallen fence is often more urgent than it looks. A gap in a boundary can let children or pets out, leave a site open, or put a heavy panel at risk of falling onto a footpath or a car. Making the area safe comes first, by laying down or securing loose panels and closing the gap where possible.

Requests for help with a fallen fence are handled by arrangement. iComply does not promise attendance times, but it will tell you honestly when a visit can be made. A temporary fix, such as propping, securing panels or closing the gap with temporary fencing, may be arranged before the permanent repair.

Most fences fall because the posts have failed at ground level or because high winds have caught solid panels. The cause is checked so the repair deals with it, rather than simply standing the old fence back up on the same failed posts.

After storms, concrete posts and gravel boards, heavier or slatted panels, and closeboard built in place are often recommended for exposed boundaries, because they cope better with wind than lightweight panels on timber posts.

Repairs to fence start with finding the cause. A leaning section, a broken panel or a sagging gate may come from a failed post, a loose fixing, wind damage, vehicle impact, tree roots or simple age. Fixing the cause matters, otherwise the same failure returns.

Storm damage often affects several bays at once. Panels blown out, posts snapped at ground level and gates wrenched off their hinges are common after high winds. Making the boundary safe comes first, followed by a permanent repair once materials are available.

Many repairs are local. Single panels, boards, pales, mesh panels, rails and fixings can usually be replaced without disturbing the rest of the line, provided matching parts are available. The repair is matched to the existing material, height and finish as closely as possible.

Repairs involving steel include treating any cut, drilled or welded areas with a zinc-rich primer or cold galvanising before any topcoat. Leaving bare steel exposed causes rust to spread under the remaining coating.

Posts for closeboard are usually treated timber or slotted concrete. Timber posts are commonly 100 mm square for standard heights, and concrete posts with mortices take arris rails and last longer at ground level. A gravel board at the base, in timber or concrete, keeps the featheredge boards off the soil so they do not wick up moisture and rot.

Steel posts for mesh and palisade systems follow the manufacturer's size, spacing and foundation guidance. Base-plated posts are bolted to existing concrete or slabs where digging is not possible, using fixings chosen for the base, and are only used where the base can take the load.

Mixed-use sites, such as flats above shops or yards behind offices, often need more than one fence type: a secure service yard, a tidy frontage and a private garden area. The scope sets out each run separately.

Landlords and agents often need fencing work coordinated with tenants. Access dates, keys, pets and parking are agreed in advance, and photos of the finished work can be supplied for the property file.

Homeowners usually want a fence that looks good, gives privacy and lasts. Landlords and managing agents want something durable and easy to maintain across several properties. Businesses want security and a tidy frontage. The same survey approach works for all of them, with the specification adjusted to suit.

Shared boundaries are common in terraced and semi-detached housing. Agreeing the line, the height and the finished face with the neighbour before work starts avoids disputes later. The owner makes that agreement; iComply fences to the line it is given.

Where a specification, insurer or landlord sets requirements for a fence, the scope refers to them and the products are chosen to meet them. Certification of a product belongs to its manufacturer; iComply supplies and installs to the maker's instructions.

Work is carried out with risk assessments appropriate to the job, care around buried services and protection for lawns, paving and planting next to the line. Operatives follow site rules and inductions on commercial, school and industrial premises.

Waste from fencing work, including old panels, posts, concrete and offcuts, is removed from site as part of the agreed scope. Where materials can be recycled, they are separated and taken to the appropriate facility.

iComply does not promise attendance or completion times in advance. Visits and installation dates are agreed directly with you, and you are kept informed if weather or ground conditions change the plan on the day.

Conventionally the finished face of a boundary fence faces outwards, towards the neighbour or the road, with the posts and rails on the owner's side. The scope records the agreed direction.
What happens to the old fence?
It is taken down and removed from site unless you ask to keep any part of it. Removal is written into the scope.
Can you come out today?
We do not promise attendance times. Contact us with photos and we will tell you honestly when a visit can be made.
Should I try to stand the fence back up?
Only if it is safe. Laying panels flat or securing them is usually safer until the posts are repaired.
Do you work for landlords and managing agents?
Yes. We coordinate access with tenants and can supply photos of completed work for your records.

fence-post-repair.seo_title: Fence Post Repair | iComply Property Services
fence-post-repair.meta_desc: Fence Post Repair: timber, concrete and steel posts set, reset or replaced so the fence stands straight. Survey and written scope from Stockport. Quote POA.
fence-post-repair.intro: Fence Post Repair: timber, concrete and steel posts set, reset or replaced so the fence stands straight. iComply works for homeowners, landlords and residents' management companies from its Stockport workshop, measures before it specifies, and quotes every job price on application. It covers how damage is assessed, when a repair is sensible and when replacement is the better value.
fence-post-repair.body:
Fence post repair covers a single leaning or rotten post as well as several along a run. This page explains repair spurs, resetting posts, replacing posts within an existing fence and knowing when the run needs replacing.

Concrete fence posts are a long-lasting replacement for timber in panel fences. Slotted concrete posts hold panels in grooves, and mortice posts take arris rails for closeboard. Both are heavy and need careful handling and setting, but they do not rot, and they are the usual choice when timber posts have already failed once.

Fence posts carry the whole fence, so when a fence leans or falls it is usually the posts that have failed. Timber posts rot at ground level, where air, water and soil meet. Concrete posts crack or snap when panels are forced or when the fence takes a heavy blow. Steel posts loosen if the foundation is too shallow or the ground is soft.

A concrete repair spur is a short concrete post set in the ground beside a rotten timber post and bolted to it. It saves taking the fence down and suits fences where the panels or boards are still sound. It is a repair rather than a replacement, and the scope says so.

Post depth is roughly a quarter to a third of the fence height below ground, more on exposed sites or soft ground. Posts are set in concrete or compacted hardcore, depending on the system and the ground, and are plumbed in two directions and braced while the foundation sets.

Replacing a post means breaking out or working around the old foundation. Where the old concrete can be removed, the new post goes in the same position. Where it cannot, the new post is set alongside, which may mean adjusting the panel or rail fixings. The approach depends on what is found when the ground is opened.

Vehicle damage on commercial and industrial sites tends to bend posts, rails and pales. Bent steel is replaced rather than straightened where its strength or finish has been compromised, and protection such as bollards or barriers is suggested where impacts keep happening.

A repair quote sets out what has failed, why, what is being replaced and what is being left. Where the remaining parts are near the end of their life, the quote says so honestly, so the decision between repair and replacement is an informed one.

Storm damage often affects several bays at once. Panels blown out, posts snapped at ground level and gates wrenched off their hinges are common after high winds. Making the boundary safe comes first, followed by a permanent repair once materials are available.

Repairs involving steel include treating any cut, drilled or welded areas with a zinc-rich primer or cold galvanising before any topcoat. Leaving bare steel exposed causes rust to spread under the remaining coating.

Insurance claims for fence damage often need photos and a written description. iComply can provide photos of the damage and a written scope and quote to support a claim; the claim itself is between the owner and the insurer.

Many repairs are local. Single panels, boards, pales, mesh panels, rails and fixings can usually be replaced without disturbing the rest of the line, provided matching parts are available. The repair is matched to the existing material, height and finish as closely as possible.

The specification for fence posts is usually described in a handful of terms: height, material, profile or panel type, post type and foundation, finish and colour, and gate details. When comparing quotes, checking each of those terms side by side shows whether two prices are for the same thing.

iComply quotes fence posts price on application after a survey or after reviewing clear photos and measurements. There are no headline prices, because the cost depends on length, height, ground, access and specification, all of which differ from site to site.

Good access makes installation simpler. Clear routes for materials, somewhere to unload, room to work on both sides of the line and a plan for any planting or structures near the boundary all help. The survey notes access so the plan is realistic.

Most failed fences fail at the posts. Timber posts rot at ground level, concrete posts crack where a panel has been forced, and steel posts loosen in shallow or soft foundations. Looking at the posts first tells you whether the job is a repair, a part replacement or a new line, and that decision is written down before anything is ordered.

Panel fence repairs are usually about replacing blown or rotten panels, swapping split timber posts for concrete, or setting a leaning post upright. Where only one or two panels have failed, matching the style and colour of the remaining fence is part of the job.

Residential access is often tight. Materials may need carrying through a side passage or even through the house, and gardens need protecting during the work. Access is noted at the survey so the plan is realistic.

Neighbours share most residential boundaries. Talking to the neighbour before work starts, agreeing the line and height, and deciding which way the finished face points all help the job go smoothly.

For homes, a fence is part of the garden as much as the boundary. Height, style, colour and how it suits planting and paving matter as much as strength. A survey covers the look you want as well as the practical needs.

Residents' management companies and landlords often look after shared boundaries on estates and blocks. Consistency of style across the estate, tenant access and budgets for planned work are part of the conversation.

Pets and children affect the specification. Gaps under fences, gates that do not close properly and climbable rails are the usual concerns, and the scope addresses them directly.

Waste from fencing work, including old panels, posts, concrete and offcuts, is removed from site as part of the agreed scope. Where materials can be recycled, they are separated and taken to the appropriate facility.

Where a specification, insurer or landlord sets requirements for a fence, the scope refers to them and the products are chosen to meet them. Certification of a product belongs to its manufacturer; iComply supplies and installs to the maker's instructions.

Every fencing job is quoted price on application. The quote follows a survey or a review of clear photos and measurements and is based on a written scope, so you can see exactly what is included before agreeing to anything.

iComply does not promise attendance or completion times in advance. Visits and installation dates are agreed directly with you, and you are kept informed if weather or ground conditions change the plan on the day.

faq: Is it worth repairing or should I replace?

If most of the posts and panels are sound, repair is usually sensible. If many posts have failed or the materials are near the end of their life, replacement is often better value. The quote explains which.
Can you help with an insurance claim?
We can provide photos and a written scope and quote to support a claim. The claim itself is between you and your insurer.
Do I need my neighbour's permission?
For a fence on your own land, usually not, but agreeing the line and finished face with your neighbour avoids disputes. Shared boundaries need agreement.
Can you replace fence posts without replacing the fence?
Often, yes. Panels or rails are taken off, the post replaced, and the fence refitted. Where many posts have failed, a new fence may be better value.
Are concrete fence posts better than timber?
They last much longer at ground level because they do not rot. They are heavier to handle but are the usual replacement when timber posts have failed.

security-fencing-for-schools.intro: Security Fencing for Schools from iComply Property Services covers steel mesh and palisade boundaries specified for the level of security a site actually needs. This guide is written for school business managers, academy trusts, nurseries and estates teams and starts from a site survey and a written scope, not a catalogue price. It sets out the options, the specification choices and the questions worth asking before you commit to security fencing.
security-fencing-for-schools.body:
Security fencing for schools balances safeguarding with a welcoming site. This page explains how school security fencing is specified, which mesh and railing systems suit schools, and how entrances and gates are planned.

Some specifications ask for products certified to a recognised security standard, such as LPS 1175 or Secured by Design. Where a specification calls for that, iComply supplies and fits the certified product to the manufacturer's installation instructions. iComply does not certify fences itself, and a certification belongs to the product as tested, not to the installer.

A security fencing survey records the boundary length, the ground, the threats the owner is worried about, existing cameras and lighting, gate and access needs, and any planning or neighbour constraints. The written scope then sets out the system, height, fixings, toppings and gates, with the price on application.

Gates are usually the weakest point of a security fence. A manual gate in a security line needs matching infill, robust hinges that cannot be lifted off, a lock that cannot be reached through the infill, and a drop bolt or keep set into a proper foundation. Powered gates belong to a separate specification and are scoped separately.

Fixings matter as much as the panel. Security systems use tamper-resistant bolts, clamp bars and shear nuts so panels cannot simply be unbolted from outside. The fixing side normally faces into the site. On palisade, the pale fixings, rail-to-post brackets and post caps all need to be the anti-tamper type for the fence to perform as intended.

Delay is the honest way to think about a security fence. No fence stops a determined intruder with tools indefinitely; a good fence makes climbing and cutting slower, noisier and more visible, which gives cameras, alarms and people time to act. That is why security fencing is often specified alongside CCTV, lighting and access control rather than on its own.

A written scope protects both sides. It lists what is included, what is excluded, how waste is removed, how the site is left and what happens if something unexpected is found. With security fencing, as with most building work, the clearer the scope, the fewer disagreements at the end.

The specification for security fencing is usually described in a handful of terms: height, material, profile or panel type, post type and foundation, finish and colour, and gate details. When comparing quotes, checking each of those terms side by side shows whether two prices are for the same thing.

Most buyers underestimate how much the ground affects the job. A level lawn, a sloping bank, a tarmac car park and a strip of made ground beside a building all need different post and foundation methods. Asking how the posts will be set, and what happens if buried services or old concrete are found, avoids surprises.

iComply quotes security fencing price on application after a survey or after reviewing clear photos and measurements. There are no headline prices, because the cost depends on length, height, ground, access and specification, all of which differ from site to site.

Before choosing security fencing, it helps to write down what the boundary must achieve. Privacy, security, keeping children or animals in, marking a line, screening bins or plant, and meeting a landlord's or insurer's requirement all point to different products. A short list of priorities makes the survey quicker and the recommendation clearer.

iComply does not publish price lists, because a headline price cannot reflect the ground, the access and the specification on your site. Every job is quoted price on application after a survey or a review of clear photos and measurements.

Ground and access often make the biggest difference between two similar-looking jobs. Digging through tarmac, concrete, roots or made ground takes longer than digging in clear soil, and materials carried by hand through a house cost more to install than materials unloaded beside the line.

The cost of security fencing depends on a handful of factors: the length of the run, the height, the material and system, the number and type of gates, the ground conditions, access for materials and the amount of old fence to remove. Change any of those and the price changes.

358 panels are heavy and rigid, so they are fixed to strong posts with continuous clamp bars and security bolts. On higher-risk sites, a double-skin arrangement or a second layer at the bottom of the fence is sometimes specified to add delay. Toppings such as razor wire or rotating spikes can be added where they are justified and signed.

Finish is usually hot-dip galvanising, which protects the steel against corrosion for many years. A polyester powder coat can be applied over galvanising for colour, commonly green or black, and adds a further layer. Galvanised-only palisade weathers to a dull grey. Any cutting or drilling on site is treated with a zinc-rich paint so rust does not start at the cut.

Schools and nurseries need fencing that supports safeguarding: a continuous secure line, controlled entrances, no gaps and no climbing aids. The layout is agreed with the school's leadership and estates team.

Academy trusts and local authorities often need detailed written quotes and specifications for funding and procurement. The scope is written to support those processes.

Durability and low maintenance matter for school budgets. Galvanised and powder-coated mesh and railings last many years with little upkeep, which is why they are the usual choice for school boundaries.

Work at schools is planned around term dates, the school run and safeguarding procedures. Holiday and out-of-hours working is common, and operatives follow sign-in and site rules.

Waste from fencing work, including old panels, posts, concrete and offcuts, is removed from site as part of the agreed scope. Where materials can be recycled, they are separated and taken to the appropriate facility.

faq: What should I decide before getting a quote?
Write down what the fence must achieve, the rough length and height you have in mind, and any gates. The survey then confirms the details and the right specification.
Why is there no price list?
Cost depends on length, height, ground, access and specification. Every job is quoted price on application from a written scope.
Can you work around term dates?
Yes. Most school fencing work is planned for holidays or out of hours, with safeguarding procedures followed.
How high should a security fence be?
Commercial security fences are commonly 1.8 m to 3.0 m. The height is chosen from the risk, the site and any planning limits, and taller fences need stronger posts and foundations.
Is palisade or mesh more secure?

Both can be specified to a high level. Palisade is strong and familiar; welded mesh such as 358 is hard to climb and cut and keeps good visibility for cameras. The choice depends on the site, the look and the specification.

palisade-fencing-for-warehouses.intro: Palisade Fencing for Warehouses from iComply Property Services covers vertical steel pales on horizontal rails, specified by pale profile, top and height.
