palisade-fencing-for-warehouses.body:
Palisade fencing for warehouses has to cope with HGVs, large yards and valuable stock. This page explains palisade specifications for warehouse boundaries, vehicle gates, impact protection and phasing around yard operations.

Damage to palisade is usually local: a bent or cut pale, a rail knocked off by a vehicle, a leaning post or a missing fixing. Because each pale is bolted on individually, single pales and rails can normally be replaced without taking down the run, provided the new parts match the profile, height and finish.

Palisade is installed post by post along a string line. Posts are set in concrete at the spacing the rails require, rails are bolted to the posts with security brackets, and pales are fixed to the rails with anti-tamper bolts or shear nuts facing into the site. On slopes, palisade is usually raked so the pales stay vertical and the rails follow the ground.

Typical palisade heights are 1.8 m, 2.1 m, 2.4 m and 3.0 m, with lower and taller options in some ranges. The height affects the number of rails, the post size and the foundation. A 3.0 m run carries noticeably more load from its own weight and from people leaning or climbing than a 1.8 m run, so the posts and concrete are sized accordingly.

A palisade scope lists the run length, height, pale profile and top, post size and foundation, rail count, fixings, finish and colour, gate details and any toppings. It is priced on application after the site has been walked and the ground assessed.

There are two main pale profiles. D-section pales are a curved, D-shaped section suited to lower-risk boundaries and general demarcation. W-section pales are folded into a W shape, which makes them stiffer and harder to cut, and they are normally chosen for security boundaries. The two are not interchangeable on the same rail fixings without checking.

Before choosing palisade fencing, it helps to write down what the boundary must achieve. Privacy, security, keeping children or animals in, marking a line, screening bins or plant, and meeting a landlord's or insurer's requirement all point to different products. A short list of priorities makes the survey quicker and the recommendation clearer.

The specification for palisade fencing is usually described in a handful of terms: height, material, profile or panel type, post type and foundation, finish and colour, and gate details. When comparing quotes, checking each of those terms side by side shows whether two prices are for the same thing.

Lifespan depends on the material and the care it gets. Timber needs treatment and will eventually need parts replaced. Galvanised and powder-coated steel lasts much longer with little maintenance. Asking what maintenance the chosen option needs, and how often, is part of choosing well.

iComply quotes palisade fencing price on application after a survey or after reviewing clear photos and measurements. There are no headline prices, because the cost depends on length, height, ground, access and specification, all of which differ from site to site.

A written scope protects both sides. It lists what is included, what is excluded, how waste is removed, how the site is left and what happens if something unexpected is found. With palisade fencing, as with most building work, the clearer the scope, the fewer disagreements at the end.

Specification choices change both the upfront cost and the lifetime cost. Concrete posts cost more than timber at the start but rarely need replacing. Powder-coated steel costs more than bare galvanised but looks better for longer. A quote that explains those trade-offs helps you choose.

The cost of palisade fencing depends on a handful of factors: the length of the run, the height, the material and system, the number and type of gates, the ground conditions, access for materials and the amount of old fence to remove. Change any of those and the price changes.

To get an accurate quote quickly, send the address, the approximate length and height, photos of the boundary and any gates, and a note of what you want the fence to achieve. A written scope and quote follow, listing what is included.

Some specifications ask for products certified to a recognised security standard, such as LPS 1175 or Secured by Design. Where a specification calls for that, iComply supplies and fits the certified product to the manufacturer's installation instructions. iComply does not certify fences itself, and a certification belongs to the product as tested, not to the installer.

Galvanising is what makes steel palisade last outdoors. The steel is dipped in molten zinc after fabrication so the coating reaches inside folds and holes. A galvanised finish weathers to a matt grey. Where colour is wanted, a powder coat is applied over the galvanising; the scope says which finish is being supplied, so there is no surprise on delivery.

Warehouses and distribution centres have large yards, high vehicle movements and valuable stock. Their boundaries need to be strong, continuous and compatible with gatehouses, barriers and camera systems. Steel palisade and heavy mesh are the usual choices.

Warehouse landlords and tenants often share responsibility for boundaries. The scope identifies who instructs the work and who approves the specification, and insurance requirements are referred to where they apply.

Vehicle impacts are common on warehouse boundaries. Fence lines next to turning areas and parking bays benefit from kerbs, barriers or bollards, and gate posts are protected where lorries pass close.

Yard operations rarely stop. Fencing work is phased around HGV movements, loading bays and shift patterns, with exclusion zones agreed with the yard manager and temporary barriers where needed.

Work is carried out with risk assessments appropriate to the job, care around buried services and protection for lawns, paving and planting next to the line. Operatives follow site rules and inductions on commercial, school and industrial premises.

fencing-for-industrial-estates.body:
Fencing for industrial estates has to serve the estate as a whole and the individual units within it. This page explains estate boundaries, unit yards, design standards and planning work around shared roads and tenants.

Underground services are a real risk on industrial land. Drainage, power cables, gas pipes and data ducts often run close to boundaries. Utility drawings are requested, the line is scanned with a cable avoidance tool before digging, and trial holes are dug by hand where services are suspected.

Industrial sites rarely stop for fencing work. Installation is phased around deliveries, shift patterns and yard movements, with exclusion zones around the working area and temporary barriers where a section of the old fence has to come down before the new one goes up. The sequence is agreed with the site manager in writing.

Industrial fencing protects yards, plant, stock and vehicles, and it has to survive forklifts, lorries reversing and years of weather. The usual systems are steel palisade and heavy welded mesh, with manual swing or sliding gates for vehicle access, and sometimes impact protection where vehicles turn close to the fence line.

Many industrial fences sit on boundaries with neighbouring businesses or public land. The line, height and toppings are agreed before work, and toppings are positioned so they do not overhang a neighbour's land or a public footway without agreement.

Vehicle gates on industrial boundaries take heavy use. Manual swing gates need strong hinges, gate stops and drop bolts set into proper keeps. Sliding gates need a clear run-back area and a level track or a cantilever arrangement. Gate leaves and posts are sized for the opening, not taken from a standard list.

Ground on industrial sites is often hard standing, made ground or old foundations. Posts may need core drilling through concrete, longer posts in made ground, or base plates where digging is not possible. These decisions affect the cost and are made on site rather than assumed.

Good access makes installation simpler. Clear routes for materials, somewhere to unload, room to work on both sides of the line and a plan for any planting or structures near the boundary all help. The survey notes access so the plan is realistic.

Planning rules, boundary agreements and lease terms can all affect industrial fencing. Height near a highway, conservation areas, listed buildings, planning conditions on newer estates and covenants on some properties are worth checking early. iComply flags the points it sees; the owner makes the checks and decisions.

Lifespan depends on the material and the care it gets. Timber needs treatment and will eventually need parts replaced. Galvanised and powder-coated steel lasts much longer with little maintenance. Asking what maintenance the chosen option needs, and how often, is part of choosing well.

iComply quotes industrial fencing price on application after a survey or after reviewing clear photos and measurements. There are no headline prices, because the cost depends on length, height, ground, access and specification, all of which differ from site to site.

Privacy, security, keeping children or animals in, marking a line, screening bins or plant, and meeting a landlord's or insurer's requirement all point to different products. A short list of priorities makes the survey quicker and the recommendation clearer.

Local work keeps travel and delivery simple. Materials are ordered for the job once the scope is agreed and delivered to site or collected from local suppliers. Waste is taken away rather than left in a skip on the street unless a skip has been agreed.

Survey visits are booked by arrangement at a time that suits the site. For homes, that is often an evening or weekend; for commercial and industrial sites, it is usually during working hours with the site manager present. No attendance time is promised in advance; the visit is agreed directly.

Covering a wide local area means iComply sees most types of boundary: terraced back yards, suburban gardens, new-build estates, schools, business parks, depots and farm land. That experience feeds into the advice given on site about which industrial fencing option suits the boundary in front of you.

Manual sliding palisade gates suit openings where there is no room for leaves to swing, or where the ground slopes across the opening. They need a clear run-back area along the fence line equal to the opening. Tracked sliding gates run on a ground rail; cantilever gates hang from rollers and leave the opening clear.

Perimeter fencing is a fence planned around the whole boundary of a site rather than a single run. The point is continuity: one weak section, an unfenced corner or a poorly fitted gate undoes the rest. A perimeter survey walks the full line and records every change in ground, every structure the fence meets and every opening.

Work on estates is planned around shared roads and other tenants' access. Deliveries, parking and work areas are agreed with the estate manager so other businesses are not disrupted.

Estate managers often plan fencing alongside other security measures, such as estate barriers, cameras and lighting. The fence line, heights and gates are coordinated with those plans.

Tenants on estates should check their lease before changing a boundary. Estate managers often have design standards for colours and profiles, which the scope follows.

Industrial estates combine many units, shared roads and different tenants. Estate-wide fencing has to be consistent in style and security, while individual units may need their own yards and gates. The scope sets out which runs are estate boundaries and which belong to individual units.

Every fencing job is quoted price on application. The quote follows a survey or a review of clear photos and measurements and is based on a written scope, so you can see exactly what is included before agreeing to anything.

anti-climb-fence-toppings-installation.intro: Anti-Climb Fence Toppings Installation from iComply Property Services covers razor wire, barbed wire, rotating spikes and spike strips fitted safely to fences, walls and gates. This guide is written for facilities managers, business owners, landlords and managing agents and starts from a site survey and a written scope, not a catalogue price. It walks through how installation is planned, from setting out and post foundations to finishing, waste removal and handover.
anti-climb-fence-toppings-installation.body:
Anti-climb fence toppings installation adds delay to the top of a fence, wall or gate. This page explains razor wire, barbed wire, rotating spikes and spike strips, how they are fitted and how duty of care shapes their position.

Rotating spike barriers are popular on walls and gates because they turn under any grip and are less visually aggressive than razor wire. Plastic spike strips are used on lower walls and fences in residential settings where a more limited deterrent is appropriate.

Anti-climb fence toppings are added to the top of a fence, wall or gate to make crossing it slower and harder. The main types are razor wire coils, barbed wire strands on cranked arms, rotating spike barriers that turn under a hand, and rigid plastic or steel spike strips. Each has different levels of deterrence and different safety considerations.

Duty of care applies to toppings. They are fitted above head height, typically above 2 m, kept away from footways and play areas where possible, and signed with clear warnings. Planning permission may be needed for some toppings in some positions, and the owner confirms that before work starts.

The fence or wall must take the extra load. Old palisade with corroded fixings or a wall with loose coping may not hold arms and wire safely. The structure is checked first and repairs are quoted where needed.

Topping repairs include replacing sagging wire, refixing loose arms and replacing damaged rotating sections. Old razor wire is removed and disposed of safely as part of the job.

Cranked arms tilt outwards or inwards from the top of the posts and carry barbed or razor wire. Outward-facing arms deter climbing in, while inward arms deter climbing out. Y-shaped arms do both. The arms are bolted to the existing posts with fixings matched to the post section.

Finishing includes fitting caps, treating any cut ends or drilled steel, checking every fixing, clearing offcuts and spoil, and leaving the ground tidy along both sides of the line. Old fencing and waste are removed from site as agreed.

Installation time depends on the length, the ground, access and the weather. The plan agreed in the scope sets out the sequence and any phasing, and the client is kept informed if conditions on the day change the plan.

Gates are hung once their posts have set firm. Hinges, latches, stops and drop bolts are fitted, and the gate is adjusted so it swings freely and closes properly. A gate that is hung on posts before the concrete has cured will often drop later.

Installation of anti-climb fence toppings starts with setting out. The line is marked with pegs and a string line from the confirmed boundary points, corners and gate positions. Panel or bay widths are worked out from the ends so cut sections fall where they are least visible, and the post positions are marked before any digging starts.

Once the posts are set, rails, panels, boards, pales or mesh are fixed in order along the run. Levels are checked as the work progresses so the top line is consistent, and adjustments are made for slopes by stepping or raking as agreed in the scope.

Replacement means taking down an existing fence and putting a new one up along the agreed line. It is the right choice when the posts have failed along much of the run, when the material has reached the end of its life, or when the owner wants a different type of fence.

On sites where the boundary cannot be left open, replacement is phased so only a short section is down at any time, or temporary fencing is used until the new line is complete.

Replacement is a good time to reconsider the specification. Concrete posts and gravel boards instead of timber, a heavier panel for an exposed garden, mesh instead of palisade for better visibility, or a different height can all be considered while the line is open.

Anti-climb fencing describes fences designed so that climbing is difficult: small mesh apertures, smooth vertical faces, no horizontal rails on the outside, and toppings that make the top hard to cross. The most common anti-climb fence is 358 mesh, often combined with a topping on higher-risk sites.

Palisade fencing is made of vertical steel pales bolted to horizontal rails, which are fixed to steel posts set in concrete. It is one of the most common commercial and industrial boundaries in the UK because it is strong, familiar and hard to climb without tools. The specification is described by pale profile, pale top, height and finish.

Commercial boundaries are often part of a wider security plan that includes cameras, lighting, access control and alarm systems. The fence specification is coordinated with those systems so camera views are not blocked and gates suit any access control planned.

Facilities managers need fencing work that fits around the business. Out-of-hours working, phased installation, clear method statements and a tidy site at the end of each day are normal requirements and are agreed before work starts.

Insurers sometimes ask for specific security measures as a condition of cover. Where an insurer or security consultant has set a requirement, the fence is specified to meet it, and the scope refers to the requirement.

Many commercial premises are leased. Tenants should check lease terms and landlord consent before changing a boundary, and managing agents often want a written specification for approval. The scope is written to support that process.

Commercial customers often need documents for their own records: insurance details, risk assessments, method statements and product information. Those are provided as part of the job.

lps-1175-fencing.body:
LPS 1175 fencing is fencing certified by the Loss Prevention Certification Board for intruder resistance. This page explains the rating system, why installation must match the tested configuration and how iComply supplies and installs certified systems.

Certified fences are heavier, more expensive and slower to install than standard systems. A survey confirms the ground, access for heavy panels, foundation design and gate details before a quote is given, and the quote names the certified system and its rating.

iComply supplies and installs LPS 1175 certified fence systems where a specification calls for them, working to the manufacturer's instructions and keeping records of the products and installation. iComply does not certify fences and does not hold LPCB certification itself; the product certificate comes from the manufacturer.

A rating belongs to the product as tested. To keep it valid, the fence must be installed with the same panels, posts, fixings, foundations and details that were tested, following the manufacturer's installation instructions. Substituting a cheaper post, a different bolt or a different panel can mean the installed fence is not the certified product.

Issue 8 of LPS 1175 uses a two-part rating, a letter for the tool category and a number for the delay time, such as A1 up to F10. Earlier issues used security ratings SR1 to SR8. Both may appear in specifications, so the scope records exactly which rating the client's specification requires.

LPS 1175 is a Loss Prevention Standard published by the Loss Prevention Certification Board (LPCB, part of BRE) for the intruder resistance of building components, including fences and gates. Products are tested by attacking them with defined tool sets for defined times, and a certified product is given a rating that describes the level of resistance it achieved.

LPS 1175 fences are used on critical sites such as utility, data, telecoms, transport and high-value storage. They are usually part of a wider security design that includes detection, cameras and access control, and the fence specification is set by the client, their security consultant or the network operator.

Most buyers underestimate how much the ground affects the job. A level lawn, a sloping bank, a tarmac car park and a strip of made ground beside a building all need different post and foundation methods. Asking how the posts will be set, and what happens if buried services or old concrete are found, avoids surprises.

Specification choices change both the upfront cost and the lifetime cost. Concrete posts cost more than timber at the start but rarely need replacing. Powder-coated steel costs more than bare galvanised but looks better for longer. A quote that explains those trade-offs helps you choose.

Ground and access often make the biggest difference between two similar-looking jobs. Digging through tarmac, concrete, roots or made ground takes longer than digging in clear soil, and materials carried by hand through a house cost more to install than materials unloaded beside the line.

iComply does not publish price lists, because a headline price cannot reflect the ground, the access and the specification on your site. Every job is quoted price on application after a survey or a review of clear photos and measurements.

Cameras, detection systems, lighting and signs work better when the fence line is straight, clear of vegetation and free of climbing aids such as bins, pallets or trees close to the fence. The rating belongs to the tested system, so posts, fixings and panels are not mixed with other parts.

Operational continuity matters. Work is phased so access for deliveries and staff is kept open, and temporary fencing is used where a section of boundary has to come down before the replacement is in place.

Industrial boundaries take heavy use. Vehicles turning close to the fence, stacked materials leaning against it and long years of weather all take their toll. Heavier posts, impact protection and robust gates are worth considering at specification stage.

Industrial sites bring their own rules: inductions, permits, vehicle movement plans and restricted areas. iComply follows site rules, provides risk assessments and method statements, and agrees exclusion zones with the site manager before work starts.
